This security release features fixes for multiple issues.

Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately.

You can download WordPress 7.1.4 from WordPress.org, or visit your WordPress Dashboard, click “Updates”, and then click “Update Now”. If you have sites that support automatic background updates, the update process will begin automatically.
WordPress 7.1.4 is a short-cycle release. The next major release will be version 7.2, currently planned for December 8th.

For more information, please visit the WordPress 7.1.4 HelpHub site.

Security updates included in this release

The security team would like to thank the following people and organizations for responsibly reporting vulnerabilities, and allowing them to be fixed in this release:

  • A weakness in the WordPress upgrade process which can lead to remote code execution during the upgrade window, reported by Umut Bayram.
  • A stored XSS with specially crafted block markup, reported by Rafie Muhammad (Awesome Motive, Inc.).
  • Privacy Data Removal Requests can be created in a way that leads to stored XSS, reported by Anthropic.
  • Multiple stored XSS issues in the Interactivity API independently discovered by AnC and DatNLQ from VietSunshine Cyber Security, rekter0 and Anas cherni, Marcel Karlsson (whoismarcel), and Weston Ruter, Jon Surrell, Alex Concha, and Luis Herranz of the WordPress Security Team.
  • A stored denial of service issue in the Interactivity API, reported by Jon Surrell of the WordPress Security Team.
  • A stored XSS in Customizer selective refresh, reported by Rafie Muhammad (Awesome Motive, Inc.).
  • A Stored XSS in the Categories block reported by Ben Bidner of the WordPress Security Team.
  • Specially crafted User Logins can lead to a stored XSS reported by Anthropic.
  • Unpublished customizer changesets can be discovered by unauthenticated users, reported by Antonio Lorensius Silaban.
  • A Stored XSS in Playlist and image blocks, reported by Ben Bidner of the WordPress Security Team.
  • Stored XSS in core/comments-pagination-next and core/comments-pagination-previous blocks, reported by Alex Concha of the WordPress Security Team.
  • Notes can be read by privileged users that lack access to edit the post the note is attached to, reported by Ramon of the WordPress Security Team.
  • An update to the bundled root certificates due to the eMudhra revocation.

Thank you to these WordPress contributors

This release was led by Aaron Jorbin and Nik Tsekouras. WordPress 7.1.4 would not have been possible without the contributions of the following people:

Aaron Jorbin, Adam Silverstein, Alex Concha, Andrew Duthie, Andrew Serong, David Arenas, Dennis Snell, Ella Van Durpe, George Mamadashvili, Isabel Brison, Jake Spurlock, Jb Audras, Jeremy Felt, John Blackbourn, Jon Surrell, Jonathan Desrosiers, Kira Song,Lance Willett, luisherranz, Marco Ciampini, marcs0h, Marin Atanasov, Mario Santos, Miguel Fonseca, Nik Tsekouras, Peter Wilson, ramonopoly, Rudy Faile, umut3806, Weston Ruter

Backports

As a courtesy, the security fixes were backported to all branches eligible to receive security fixes (currently through 4.7). As a reminder, only the most recent version of WordPress is actively supported. The backports are in progress and will ship as they become ready.

WordPress 7.2 Beta 3 has also been released, containing all applicable fixes.

WordPress 7.2 Beta 2 is ready for download and testing! 

This beta release is intended for testing and development only. Please do not install, run, or test this version of WordPress on production or mission-critical websites. Instead, use a test environment or local site to explore the new features.

The scheduled final release date for WordPress 7.2 is December 8, 2026. The full release schedule can be found here. Your help testing Beta and RC versions is vital to making this release as stable and powerful as possible. Thank you to everyone who contributes by testing!

What’s in WordPress 7.2 Beta 2?

For technical details on the issues addressed since Beta 1, see the following links:

  • Closed 7.2 WordPress Core Trac tickets since October 20, 2026
  • 7.2 Gutenberg commits since October 20, 2026

Continued Improvements to WordPress 7.2

WordPress 7.2 Beta 2 builds on the first beta with additional enhancements, bug fixes, and refinements across the administration experience and developer APIs.

Development continues on the Abilities API, including content querying, capability requirements, and improvements to schema handling and permissions. New server-side registration capabilities for DataViews and DataForm also provide developers with more ways to extend WordPress interfaces.

Additional work includes improvements to REST API flexibility, admin asset loading, and the transition to modern SVG icons throughout WordPress administration.

Learn more: Trac #66268, Trac #66325, Trac #66229, Trac #66343, Trac #57548, Trac #65089

How important is your testing?

Testing for issues is a critical part of developing any software, and it’s a meaningful way for anyone to contribute – whether or not you have experience. Details on what to test in WordPress 7.2 are available here.

If you encounter an issue, please share it in the Alpha/Beta area of the support forums. If you are comfortable submitting a reproducible bug report, you can do so via WordPress Trac. You can also check your issue against this list of known bugs.

Curious about testing releases in general and how to get started? Follow along with the testing initiatives in Make Core and join the #core-test channel on Making WordPress Slack.

The PHP project has announced a security release that fixes two critical security vulnerabilities discovered in PHP.

Due to the critical severity of the issues, site owners are encouraged to immediately update their installations of PHP. Your web host may already be working to update PHP and put web application firewall (WAF) rules in place to mitigate the vulnerabilities, but you should still check for updates from your web host and, if necessary, update PHP as soon as possible.

Within WordPress, you can see which version of PHP your site runs under Tools > Site Health > Info > Server. Many web hosts provide this information in your web hosting administration panel too.

These vulnerabilities are not specific to WordPress and affect any server that hosts a PHP application. No WordPress update is required or planned for these issues.

Versions of PHP prior to 8.2 no longer receive security updates from the PHP project.

If your site runs a version prior to this and you manage your own web hosting, you should consider taking your server offline while you prepare to update to a newer version of PHP. This advice is being published by several national cyber security agencies. To quote the UK National Cyber Security Centre:

Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.

Building on the responsive design improvements introduced in WordPress 7.1, WordPress 7.2 expands viewport-specific styling to additional design tools and blocks. Creators gain more granular control over how layouts and visual settings adapt across screen sizes, including responsive Gallery settings for columns, image cropping, and aspect ratios.

Learn more: GitHub #80388, #82003

Improved Global Styles and Design Tools

WordPress 7.2 makes site-wide styling easier to manage with a new Customized filter for finding blocks with modified styles and inherited Global Styles values displayed directly in block inspector controls. Expanded design tools and support for styling form elements provide additional flexibility when creating a consistent visual identity across a site.

Learn more: GitHub #82520, #76525, #34198, #84657

Text Shadow Support

WordPress 7.2 introduces new text shadow controls, giving creators more ways to add depth and emphasis to their content. Text shadows can be customized through block settings and defined as presets in theme.json, making it easier to maintain consistent typography across a site.

Learn more: GitHub #73320, GitHub #79584, Trac #65869

Easier Navigation Management

Improvements to the Site Editor make managing navigation links more intuitive. Creators can add, organize, and edit navigation items directly from the editor sidebar, making it easier to maintain site menus without interrupting their editing workflow.

Learn more: GitHub #77069

Better Collaboration with Notes

WordPress 7.2 introduces Emoji reactions on notes and a new toolbar icon that makes Notes easier to access and manage. Notes move to the editor canvas, bringing conversations directly into the margin. Users can now keep Notes and the block settings sidebar open simultaneously, making it easier to review feedback while editing content.

A new minimized Notes mode reduces visual clutter, while improvements to positioning and display create a smoother, more consistent collaboration experience.

Learn more: GitHub #79970, GitHub #83786, GitHub #80015, Trac #64638

Faster, More Efficient Media Uploads

WordPress 7.2 expands client-side media processing to the Media Library, allowing images to be resized, compressed, and converted directly in the browser before being uploaded. This can improve upload performance, reduce server resource usage, and provide better support for modern image formats, particularly on hosting environments with limited image-processing capabilities.

Learn more: Trac #65661, GitHub #12585

New “On This Day” Dashboard Widget

WordPress 7.2 introduces a new On This Day dashboard widget that helps users rediscover content published on the same date in previous years. By highlighting posts from the site’s history, the widget makes it easier to revisit past content, celebrate milestones, and find opportunities to refresh or reshare older posts.

Learn more: Trac #65116

Block Editor Usability Improvements

WordPress 7.2 includes a collection of smaller improvements aimed at reducing friction in everyday editing. These changes include clearer error messages, more helpful feedback when something goes wrong, and refinements to common editor interactions, making the editing experience more predictable and approachable.

Learn more: GitHub #81453, #82496, #84656, #84649

A More Consistent WordPress Admin

WordPress 7.2 continues modernizing the administration experience by replacing legacy Dashicons in the admin bar and sidebar with icons from the WordPress icon library. The updated icons bring greater visual consistency between the traditional WordPress dashboard and newer editing interfaces.

Learn more: GitHub #12270

An Updated Block Settings Experience

A new DataForm-powered inspector introduces a refreshed approach to managing block settings in the editor. Built on the DataForm component system, this work aims to provide more consistent controls and a more extensible foundation for future block editing improvements.

Learn more: GitHub Gutenberg · Call for Testing

Faster WordPress Administration

WordPress 7.2 improves admin performance by modernizing how scripts and stylesheets are loaded. Instead of combining assets into large files, WordPress now loads them individually for better browser caching. A new prefetching mechanism also anticipates which admin screen users are likely to visit next, loading its resources in advance to make navigation between the dashboard, post lists, and editor faster.

Learn more: Trac #57548

For Developers

New Secrets API

WordPress 7.2 introduces a Secrets API, providing developers with a standardized, secure way to store sensitive credentials such as API keys and authentication tokens. The API supports encryption at rest, credential rotation, and customizable storage providers, helping plugins and integrations manage sensitive information more securely.

Learn more (Trac #66187)

Random Content Redirects

WordPress 7.2 adds support for random content redirects, allowing visitors to discover a randomly selected post through a dedicated URL. This provides a simple way to encourage content exploration and help readers rediscover older posts.

Learn more: Trac #64498

More Powerful APIs for Developers

WordPress 7.2 expands the Abilities API with new capabilities for accessing and querying WordPress data, providing a more consistent foundation for integrations, automation, and AI-powered tools. (Trac #66268, #64605, #64657)

Enhancements to the Interactivity API introduce new ways to render trusted HTML and manage reactive navigation, giving developers more flexibility when building dynamic, interactive blocks. (Trac #66246, Gutenberg PR #83092)

Additional improvements to the HTML API, block supports, and responsive design tools provide more reliable markup processing and greater control over how custom blocks are styled and displayed across devices. (Trac #65824, #66150, #65869)

How important is your testing?

Testing for issues is a critical part of developing any software, and it’s a meaningful way for anyone to contribute – whether or not you have experience. Details on what to test in WordPress 7.2 are available here.

If you encounter an issue, please share it in the Alpha/Beta area of the support forums. If you are comfortable submitting a reproducible bug report, you can do so via WordPress Trac. You can also check your issue against this list of known bugs.

Curious about testing releases in general and how to get started? Follow along with the testing initiatives in Make Core and join the #core-test channel on Making WordPress Slack.

WordPress 7.2 will include new features that were previously only available in the Gutenberg plugin. Learn more about Gutenberg updates since WordPress 7.1 in the What’s New in Gutenberg posts for versions 23.7, 23.8, 23.9, 24.0, 24.1, 24.2, and 24.3.

What’s new in WordPress 7.2?

With so much in progress for WordPress 7.2 Beta 1, this is still only the beginning; expect continued refinement with each Beta and RC release ahead of the final release on December 8, 2026

Just for you: a Beta 1 haiku:

Ipsum takes the stage
Secrets bloom, designs take shape
New blocks come alive

Props to @audrasjb, @annezazu, @adamsilverstein, @westonruter, @markoserb, @im3dabasia1, @jorbin, and @noruzzaman for proofreading and review.

This security and maintenance release features 7 security fixes and 4 bug fixes.

Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately.

You can download WordPress 7.1.3 from WordPress.org, or visit your WordPress Dashboard, click “Updates”, and then click “Update Now”. If you have sites that support automatic background updates, the update process will begin automatically.

Security updates included in this release

The security team would like to thank the following people and organizations for responsibly reporting vulnerabilities, and allowing them to be fixed in this release:

  • A stored XSS on the Comments administration page, exploitable via pending comments, reported by Trail of Bits in collaboration with OpenAI.
  • A DoS issue in the WP_Http::make_absolute_url() method, reported by Anthropic
  • A second-Order SQL injection in WordPress WXR export, reported by Anthropic
  • A weakness allowing Author role users to sticky posts, reported by Anthropic
  • Unauthenticated disclosure of comments on private & unpublished posts, reported by Ananda Dhakal from Patchstack
  • Imgur embeds are vulnerable to XSS, reported by Zhengyu Liu, Jingcheng Yang, and Gavin Zhong
  • Forgeable parameters passed to the {status}_{type} hook can lead to action name collision, reported by Alex Concha of the WordPress security team

Thank you to these WordPress contributors

This release was led by Jake Spurlock.

WordPress 7.1.3 would not have been possible without the contributions of the following people. Their asynchronous coordination to deliver maintenance and security fixes into a stable release is a testament to the power and capability of the WordPress community.

Aaron Jorbin, Adam Silverstein, Adi Moldovan, Adrian Duffell, Alex Concha, Arkaprabha Chowdhury, Deepak Kumar, donniam, Ehtisham Siddiqui, Jake Spurlock, Jb Audras, Jeremy Felt, Joe Dolson, John Blackbourn, Jon Surrell, Jonathan Desrosiers, Ken Gagne, Khokan Sardar, Lance Willett, lucatume, marcs0h, Peter Wilson, Paul Kevan, RS Software, Rudy Faile, Sergey Biryukov, siliconforks, smerriman, Stephen Bernhardt, Suryakant Upadhyay, vortfu, webVerts, Weston Ruter, Yogesh Bhutkar

Backports

As a courtesy, the security fixes are being backported, where necessary, to all branches eligible to receive security fixes (currently through 4.7). As a reminder, only the most recent version of WordPress is actively supported. The backports are in progress and will ship as they become ready.

How to contribute

To get involved in WordPress core development, head over to Trac, pick a ticket, and join the conversation in the #core channel. Need help? Check out the Core Contributor Handbook.

This security release features a fix for a critical severity security vulnerability.

Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately.

You can download WordPress 7.1.2 from WordPress.org, or visit your WordPress Dashboard, click “Updates”, and then click “Update Now”. If you have sites that support automatic background updates, the update process will begin automatically.

Security update included in this release

The security team would like to thank Robert Ressl for responsibly disclosing that an unauthenticated attacker can, under certain conditions, make page template resolution include a chosen readable local PHP file outside the active theme directories. If relevant pre-conditions for both the server environment and the active theme are met, this can lead to remote code execution (RCE).

Thank you to these WordPress contributors

This release was led by John Blackbourn. WordPress 7.1.2 would not have been possible without the contributions of the following people:

Aaron Jorbin, Aki Hamano, Alex Concha, Ehtisham Siddiqui, fiocavallari, Jb Audras, Jeffrey Paul, Jeremy Felt, Joe McGill, John Blackbourn, Jon Surrell, Lance Willett, Manuel Camargo, marcs0h, martin.krcho, Mukesh Panchal, Olga Gleckler, Pascal Birchler, Peter Wilson, Rajin Sharwar, Ressl, Rudy Faile, Sergey Biryukov, Shail Mehta, Stephanie Walters, and vortfu.

CVE and GHSA references

Further details can be found in the advisory: CVE-2026-87902 / GHSA-7hp8-65ch-5whp.

Backports

As a courtesy, the security fix was backported to all branches eligible to receive security fixes (currently through 4.7). As a reminder, only the most recent version of WordPress is actively supported.

I’m happy to announce that I am now serving as president of the Open Website Alliance (OWA), representing the WordPress Foundation. The Alliance brings together the community organizations behind Drupal, Joomla!, TYPO3, and WordPress to advocate for open source and share practices that benefit their projects. I represent the WordPress Foundation in this role, which rotates among the Alliance’s members.

WordPress announced its participation in the Alliance in 2024, building on our work with Drupal, Joomla!, and TYPO3 to respond to the European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act. While many open source projects focus on underlying digital infrastructure, our content management systems power the websites where businesses reach customers and sell products and services. We asked policymakers to account for that economic role when setting security requirements, while respecting how communities of developers, translators, educators, and other contributors build and maintain the software. We share a belief that everyone should have the freedom to use, change, and share the tools they rely on.

This commitment to openness builds on efforts such WordPress’s recent signing of the Open Weights and American AI Leadership letter. Our mission to democratize publishing means giving anyone a voice and welcoming everyone to contribute. Working with other communities puts those values into practice beyond WordPress, supporting the freedoms that make participation possible. I invite you to read the Open Website Alliance charter to learn more about the commitments its members share and how the Alliance works.

This security and maintenance release features 17 bug fixes on Core, 19 bug fixes for the Block Editor, and 11 security fixes.

Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately.

You can download WordPress 7.1.1 from WordPress.org, or visit your WordPress Dashboard, click “Updates”, and then click “Update Now”. If you have sites that support automatic background updates, the update process will begin automatically.

WordPress 7.1.1 is a short-cycle release. The next major release will be version 7.2 and is currently planned for December.

For more information, please visit the WordPress 7.1.1 HelpHub site.

Security updates included in this release

The security team would like to thank the following people for responsibly reporting vulnerabilities, and allowing them to be fixed in this release:

  • Stored cross-site scripting in wpautop() allows an unauthenticated visitor to inject script (subject to comment approval), reported by Rafie Muhammad (Awesome Motive, Inc.).
  • HTML API: set_modifiable_text() allows breaking out of a comment via abrupt-closing sequences, reported by Jeremy Felt of the WordPress Security Team.
  • Stored XSS in some themes that support custom headers, reported by Jeremy Felt of the WordPress Security Team.
  • Specially crafted URLs can automatically install and preview an inactive theme from WordPress.org, reported by Paulos Yibelo and pwn.ai.
  • Site Administrator can network-activate an installed Network-only plugin, reported by Jesse McNeil.
  • Authenticated Path Traversal in WP REST Templates Controller, reported by Anthropic.
  • XML-RPC can be used to publish customize_changeset posts that bypass checks for edit_css, reported by Ben Bidner of the WordPress Security Team.
  • Contributor+ Arbitrary Post Overwrite, reported by Anthropic.
  • Missing read_post check in attachment_submitbox_metadata() leaks a private parent-post title, reported by HDWSec.
  • Missing Authorization leads to Draft/Pending Post Slug Disclosure by Contributor+, reported by Jakub Herman.
  • Comments, including notes, can be reparented by any authenticated user, reported by Justin Hart, Viridis Security.

Thank you to these WordPress contributors

This release was led by Adam Silverstein, Adrian Duffell, Andrei Draganescu, and Aaron Jorbin.

WordPress 7.1.1 would not have been possible without the contributions of the following people. Their asynchronous coordination to deliver maintenance and security fixes into a stable release is a testament to the power and capability of the WordPress community.

As a courtesy, the security fixes are being backported, where necessary, to all branches eligible to receive security fixes (currently through 4.7). As a reminder, only the most recent version of WordPress is actively supported. The backports are in progress and will ship as they become ready.

How to contribute

To get involved in WordPress core development, head over to Trac, pick a ticket, and join the conversation in the #core channel. Need help? Check out the Core Contributor Handbook.

In July, students at two campuses in Kishoreganj, Bangladesh, built 108 websites. In eastern Uganda, a workshop that arrived to find no electricity at the school ran anyway, for more than 100 learners, because a former student had asked for it. In Costa Rica, three university students taught a three-session WordPress class to 40 high schoolers, then wrote down exactly how they did it so anyone else could run the same class. None of these students paid to take part, and most had never built a website before.

Those workshops came out of two programs. WordPress Campus Connect brings free, hands-on WordPress sessions to schools and universities, run by local volunteers working from a shared curriculum. WordPress Credits goes further, placing students in mentored internships where they contribute to WordPress itself and earn academic credit for the work. Credits passed 226 graduates in July, up from 199 in June, and now works with 38 partner institutions across 16 countries.

What the Students Built

The Kishoreganj series was organized by Muhibul Haque, who brought Campus Connect to two institutions two weeks apart. Students at Kishoreganj University built 38 sites in the first session. At Kishoreganj Polytechnic Institute, where guest speaker Shipon Karmakar traveled more than 80 kilometers to attend, they built nearly 70 more. The success stories page for the series counts more than 150 participating students so far, with two further institutions still to come.

A workshop in Spain took a different route to the same result. Josep Morán ran two four-hour sessions for 100 vocational students at Escola Pia Sta. Anna in Mataró, who used Playground and AI assistance to build a working plugin that calculates the best time for shore fishing in the city. Students and faculty pointed to the same two takeaways afterward: the certificate they received, and the fact that the skills map onto jobs that exist locally.

A Workshop Without Power

Bulamogi College Gadumire is on the list of Campus Connect schools in eastern Uganda because of Mariam Nairuba. At an event in Kaliro last December, she asked organizer Moses Ssebunya whether the program could come to her former school. She handled the arrangements with the administration herself, and on July 29 she navigated the team there. More than 100 learners were waiting. So was the school’s Director of Studies, who learned that day there was no electricity.

The team had brought laptops, a projector, and extension cables, none of which were useful now. Rather than cancel, they put two questions to the room instead: what do you already know about WordPress, and what would you like to know? “The room exploded,” the organizers wrote in their recap of the day. Students asked whether WordPress was free, how secure WordPress sites really are, and whether they could become developers themselves. John Wayera, one of two first-time volunteers alongside Nairuba, wrote the questions up on the blackboard as they came. The team copied down every answer. Before they left, they presented the school with a Certificate of Appreciation, which the Head Teacher received in front of the governing body.

Students Teaching Students in Costa Rica

Rita Robles Loaiza published two pilots built on the premise that the students who just learned this are the best people to teach it next. In the first, three students from the second WordPress Credits cohort at Universidad Fidélitas designed and delivered a workshop for 40 high school girls. The goal of the event is to encourage and increase female participation in STEM academic careers. Their venue was Patrones Hermosos, a science and engineering camp run by Tecnológico de Monterrey and MIT that came to Costa Rica for the first time this year. Every participant built and presented a website, satisfaction came back at 100 percent, and the team turned the whole thing into a replicable guide that any school or community group can pick up and run.

The second pilot has a longer horizon. Thirteen students at Liceo Experimental Bilingüe José Figueres Ferrer, the first high school in the Americas to join WordPress Credits, are working with the Costa Rican Spanish Polyglots team to translate WordPress into es_CR for their community service requirement. When they finish, WordPress will read a little more like home for every Costa Rican who installs it.

Get Involved

There is no cost to bring any of this to a school. Campus Connect gives an organizer a ready-made curriculum and a certificate for every student who completes it. WordPress Credits gives a student a mentor, real contributions to software that runs more than 40 percent of the web, and something concrete to put on a resume. Student Clubs give a campus group a reason to keep meeting after the workshop ends.

Education Initiatives

WordPress Education offers three practical ways for learners to develop skills, gain practical experience, and build confidence as open source contributors.

Credits
Campus Connect
Student Clubs

The full Monthly Education Buzz Report for July 2026 has the events that didn’t fit here, including a Campus Connect run entirely by students at Kyoto University of Advanced Science and a Student Club in Dhaka now organizing its own campus event.

We’re proud to announce that WordPress has signed Open Weights and American AI Leadership, an open letter asking US policymakers to not place early restrictions on open weight AI models. These are artificial intelligence models that anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure. The letter was published on July 24, 2026, and more than 270 companies and organizations have added their names. Its argument will be familiar to anyone who works in open source: technology gets better and safer when more people can study it and build on it.

That belief is the foundation WordPress is built on. Anyone can run the software, look at how it works, change it to suit their needs, and share what they make. Those freedoms are why WordPress has become a foundational part of the open web and why people trust it with their work. Open weight models bring that same kind of access to AI. A model that anyone can download and adapt becomes something people can shape around their own work and improve for everyone who comes after them.

The next generation of innovation won’t come from models alone. It will come from millions of people building with them. Open weights help make that possible. WordPress is proud to support the Open Weights and American AI Leadership letter.

– WordPress Executive Director, Mary Hubbard

Requests to US Policymakers

The requests in the letter are practical ones. As signatories, we ask policymakers to expand access to computing power for startups and researchers, to invest in shared resources like public datasets and evaluation tools, and to keep more than one kind of model available rather than narrowing the field to a handful of closed systems. We also ask that common development practices, such as using one model’s output to improve another, not be treated as theft by default. Each of these requests follows the pattern that has made open source software dependable for decades, where many people test, improve, and secure the same technology in public view.

For more than 20 years, WordPress has run on the idea that the people using a technology should be free to shape it. AI is becoming part of how people publish, and open weight models are one way that freedom carries forward. Keeping them available gives the next generation of builders, the people now learning WordPress, the same starting point that open source gave everyone before them.

This security release features fixes for multiple issues.

Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately.

You can download WordPress 7.1.4 from WordPress.org, or visit your WordPress Dashboard, click “Updates”, and then click “Update Now”. If you have sites that support automatic background updates, the update process will begin automatically.
WordPress 7.1.4 is a short-cycle release. The next major release will be version 7.2, currently planned for December 8th.

For more information, please visit the WordPress 7.1.4 HelpHub site.

Security updates included in this release

The security team would like to thank the following people and organizations for responsibly reporting vulnerabilities, and allowing them to be fixed in this release:

  • A weakness in the WordPress upgrade process which can lead to remote code execution during the upgrade window, reported by Umut Bayram.
  • A stored XSS with specially crafted block markup, reported by Rafie Muhammad (Awesome Motive, Inc.).
  • Privacy Data Removal Requests can be created in a way that leads to stored XSS, reported by Anthropic.
  • Multiple stored XSS issues in the Interactivity API independently discovered by AnC and DatNLQ from VietSunshine Cyber Security, rekter0 and Anas cherni, Marcel Karlsson (whoismarcel), and Weston Ruter, Jon Surrell, Alex Concha, and Luis Herranz of the WordPress Security Team.
  • A stored denial of service issue in the Interactivity API, reported by Jon Surrell of the WordPress Security Team.
  • A stored XSS in Customizer selective refresh, reported by Rafie Muhammad (Awesome Motive, Inc.).
  • A Stored XSS in the Categories block reported by Ben Bidner of the WordPress Security Team.
  • Specially crafted User Logins can lead to a stored XSS reported by Anthropic.
  • Unpublished customizer changesets can be discovered by unauthenticated users, reported by Antonio Lorensius Silaban.
  • A Stored XSS in Playlist and image blocks, reported by Ben Bidner of the WordPress Security Team.
  • Stored XSS in core/comments-pagination-next and core/comments-pagination-previous blocks, reported by Alex Concha of the WordPress Security Team.
  • Notes can be read by privileged users that lack access to edit the post the note is attached to, reported by Ramon of the WordPress Security Team.
  • An update to the bundled root certificates due to the eMudhra revocation.

Thank you to these WordPress contributors

This release was led by Aaron Jorbin and Nik Tsekouras. WordPress 7.1.4 would not have been possible without the contributions of the following people:

Aaron Jorbin, Adam Silverstein, Alex Concha, Andrew Duthie, Andrew Serong, David Arenas, Dennis Snell, Ella Van Durpe, George Mamadashvili, Isabel Brison, Jake Spurlock, Jb Audras, Jeremy Felt, John Blackbourn, Jon Surrell, Jonathan Desrosiers, Kira Song,Lance Willett, luisherranz, Marco Ciampini, marcs0h, Marin Atanasov, Mario Santos, Miguel Fonseca, Nik Tsekouras, Peter Wilson, ramonopoly, Rudy Faile, umut3806, Weston Ruter

Backports

Remkus argues that too many site owners are stuck in a reactive mode, only investigating issues once something breaks. Remkus walks us through the products evolution, including the 2.0 update that aimed to reimagine their dashboard experience, added public APIs, and introduced tools like MCP AI integration, empowering users to query their sites health conversationally.

[00:24:11] Nathan Wrigley: We probably should have explained that. So the plugin binds to the SaaS. The SaaS holds the data. And in that way, for example, an agency could have an overview of all the sites that they’re managing and that kind of thing?

[00:24:23] Remkus: And everything that happens on that site that is worthy of tracking and monitoring for. So again, the activity log is a good example. A WordPress activity log should not live inside the WordPress site, period. From a performance standpoint, it makes no sense. Most databases for most hosting companies have issues when you track and sort a, let’s call it a busy website.

So what we do is we asynchronously pull all of that into our dashboard. So if your site goes down for whatever reason, we have a track record of what the last things that were happening on your site.

[00:24:53] Nathan Wrigley: Oh yeah, of course.

[00:24:55] Remkus: There’s just an easier way of being in check.

[00:24:58] Nathan Wrigley: So you’d log into the SaaS, everything’s there. So if your site does have some catastrophic failure, then at least you can begin to understand what’s going on.

[00:25:06] Remkus: Yep.

[00:25:07] Nathan Wrigley: And work backwards from there?

[00:25:08] Remkus: Yep.

[00:25:08] Nathan Wrigley: I think that’s probably all the questions that I’ve got. Is there anything that we didn’t touch on that you wanted to mention?

[00:25:14] Remkus: I think what’s fun to mention is that this whole rewrite allowed us to start building add-ons as well.

So the base monitor service as we have it currently is what Scanfully is. So that’s Scanfully monitor. But we’re, and probably by the time this podcast is being aired, I think we will have, the beta available for WooCommerce checkout monitoring.

This is essentially an add-on to the base service. And what it does, we fully check everything that goes into, from is the product available in your WooCommerce, website? Can I add it to cart? Can I then go to cart? Can I then start the checkout? Can I fill out the checkout? Can I start the processing of the actual payment. So we don’t go into the payment itself? So they’re test orders, so to say.

[00:25:59] Nathan Wrigley: But the moment right before?

[00:26:01] Remkus: Yep to the moment, right before. So we’ll tell you if we can’t reach the payments provider. We’ll tell you that, but we can’t, at this moment in time, do the step beyond that.

[00:26:09] Nathan Wrigley: So how does that work then? Does it literally do that as if it’s a human being, you know?

[00:26:13] Remkus: It does.

[00:26:14] Nathan Wrigley: Is some part of your SaaS kind of opening up a browser somewhere in effect and doing that journey. Finding a product, putting it in the cart, checking the cart, and so on.

[00:26:21] Remkus: And the fun thing is you get to define what that journey looks like. So if you have a custom WooCommerce checkout, or any of the other solutions. We account for that. And you can tell us if it’s any different from what their default is, or the WooCommerce default.

And from there you get to essentially define the journey. And then the journey is stored as the thing we’re checking. And we’re doing this from the external, obviously. So it doesn’t touch any monetary things. Nothing gets charged, nothing gets booked. And the plugin that is providing the connection to our dashboard, that plugin cleans up whatever test orders were made in that process.

[00:26:56] Nathan Wrigley: Right, okay. So it’s not 3000 carts.

[00:26:58] Remkus: Yeah, we don’t, want to do that.

[00:27:00] Nathan Wrigley: Do you enable that in other ways as well? for example, I’m thinking maybe a contact form is incredibly important to somebody’s business.

[00:27:07] Remkus: Yep, that’ll be next.

[00:27:08] Nathan Wrigley: Is it possible to, outside of WordPress, visit a contact page, fill out the form fields, and then even, I don’t know, maybe even check on the other side to see if an email landed or something like that?

[00:27:17] Remkus: A part of it we’ve already solved with the email monitoring, or I should say email deliverability monitoring.

[00:27:23] Nathan Wrigley: Of course you’re on the inside there, so you can see whether that got sent.

[00:27:27] Remkus: Yes. But once we’re fully done with releasing the WooCommerce checkout monitoring, we are going to move to forms next. Because you’re right, if you have a landing pages, or a critical contact form or whatever, you need to know that that still is working as intended.

[00:27:41] Nathan Wrigley: So that’s a roadmap item. To be able to build these custom journeys, starting with WooCommerce, but more or less anything at some point. We want to see if people are going from A to B to C as we’d hoped.

[00:27:52] Remkus: Yeah, it’ll be a separate thing in the sense that WooCommerce will do a lot more than just checking the validity of the form, because that’s essentially on the WooCommerce side of things, that’s the checkout form. You fill out the form. And that’s the most similar to a general form. But yeah, we will build a separate feature inside of Scanfully that allows you to do all the types of monitoring you could possibly imagine you would need to make sure your forms are working the way you design them.

[00:28:16] Nathan Wrigley: Random question just before we end. How exciting do you find this? When you embark on the journey of building a product like this, you know, oh we’re going to do this thing, me and my friend. We’re going to do this thing, it’s going to be brilliant. And then the reality sets in, you know, it’s difficult, you’ve got to manage customers and all that kind of stuff. Do you still wake up excited by this?

[00:28:32] Remkus: Oh yeah.

[00:28:33] Nathan Wrigley: Obviously you’re not going to say the opposite. I’m just wondering if that curiosity still remains and whether or not.

[00:28:38] Remkus: It does, because there’s just so much more we can still do. And the feedback that we’re getting is very positive. And especially with this new imagination of how this should be solved with the 2.x reboot I guess is probably the best word. It just excites me on the potentials that we have.

The WooCommerce checkout monitoring is a good example, but there’s tonnes of other add-ons we have in mind where it just makes sense for you to have the Scanfully monitor as base. But there’s stuff that we can do more. We’re already gathering it in one way or another, and just to be super complete with what we’re presenting. Yeah, that excites me, yeah.

[00:29:11] Nathan Wrigley: Okay, thank you for chatting to me today. Scanfully.com. Go and check it out. Remkus, where are you apart from there? If people want to contact you, are you available on a particular platform, I don’t know, social media or email or what?

[00:29:26] Remkus: remk.us

[00:29:28] Nathan Wrigley: Nice. Of course you have that domain. Yeah. That’s lovely. In which case Remkus I will speak to you soon and thank you for chatting to us about Scanfully.

[00:29:38] Remkus: Thank you for having me.

On the podcast today we have Remkus De Vries.

Remkus has been active in the WordPress space for over twenty years, starting out with his own agency focused on high-performance, scalable WordPress websites. Over time, he has diversified into education and community-building with projects like WithinWP and a new initiative, The Guild, which is a paid community aimed at helping people build smarter, more performant sites through a first principles approach.

Our conversation centers on Scanfully, a site health and monitoring SaaS Remkus co-founded, which recently hit version 2.0. Scanfully’s focus is giving users meaningful, actionable insights into WordPress site health, security, performance, email deliverability, DNS, and more, packing all this data into an easy to understand dashboard.

We talk about Remkus’ motivation for diving deep into the complexities of WordPress monitoring, and why many users struggle to keep on top of the technical side of their websites. Remkus argues that too many site owners are stuck in reactive mode, only investigating issues once something breaks, and Scanfully aims to change that mindset by making ongoing health checks accessible and easy to parse, even for the spreadsheet-averse.

Remkus walks us through the product’s evolution, including the 2.0 update that aimed to reimagine their dashboard experience, added public APIs, and introduced tools like MCP AI integration, empowering users to query their site’s health conversationally.

We also get into recent and upcoming features such as WooCommerce checkout monitoring, activity logs, and future add-ons designed to cover forms and other business-critical flows.

If you manage multiple WordPress sites, run an agency, or are simply interested in building more robust, future-proof WordPress projects, this episode is for you.

bbPress 2.6.21 is a security and maintenance release. Everyone running bbPress should update.

This release strengthens access control across forum feeds, search results, BuddyPress activity, group forums, attachment requests, topic moves, and old topic and reply redirects. Inherited forum passwords now apply consistently when WordPress renders topic and reply content, and Akismet moderation requests now require HTTPS.

Maintenance fixes improve forum freshness and child-count queries, preserve metadata when database lookups fail, tighten route and user-profile handling, retain original dates and revision content during moderation and editing, and correct the administration reply destination controls. This release also repairs straightforward orphaned list items on WordPress 6.9 and newer, keeps generated bbPress excerpts available without duplicating content, adds the ugc relationship to topic and reply links, and refreshes administration icons for WordPress 7.2 and newer.

bbPress 2.6.21 still requires WordPress 6.0 or newer and PHP 7.2 or newer, and is tested through WordPress 7.1. The database version remains 264, so no database upgrade is required. The 2.6.21 upgrade notes cover compatibility details.

These changes are also in the 2.7 development branch, which remains 2.7.0-alpha-4. Thank you to antaloaalonso, arielmeadow, bor0, Clorith, dd32, deborah86, diddledani, lmstearn, netweb, noruzzaman, Otto42, Pebbleontheshore, r-a-y, rollybueno, sbask, shadow043, SirLouen, softglaze, terresquall, tharsheblows, and ton-ha for reports, patches, testing, and review.

Download bbPress 2.6.21 from WordPress.org, or update from your WordPress dashboard.

WordPress 7.2 Beta 2 is ready for download and testing! 

This beta release is intended for testing and development only. Please do not install, run, or test this version of WordPress on production or mission-critical websites. Instead, use a test environment or local site to explore the new features.

How to Test WordPress 7.2 Beta 2

You can test WordPress 7.2 Beta 2 in any of the following ways:

The scheduled final release date for WordPress 7.2 is December 8, 2026. The full release schedule can be found here. Your help testing Beta and RC versions is vital to making this release as stable and powerful as possible. Thank you to everyone who contributes by testing!

What’s in WordPress 7.2 Beta 2?

For technical details on the issues addressed since Beta 1, see the following links:

  • Closed 7.2 WordPress Core Trac tickets since October 20, 2026
  • 7.2 Gutenberg commits since October 20, 2026

Continued Improvements to WordPress 7.2

WordPress 7.2 Beta 2 builds on the first beta with additional enhancements, bug fixes, and refinements across the administration experience and developer APIs.

Development continues on the Abilities API, including content querying, capability requirements, and improvements to schema handling and permissions. New server-side registration capabilities for DataViews and DataForm also provide developers with more ways to extend WordPress interfaces.

Additional work includes improvements to REST API flexibility, admin asset loading, and the transition to modern SVG icons throughout WordPress administration.

Learn more: Trac #66268, Trac #66325, Trac #66229, Trac #66343, Trac #57548, Trac #65089

How important is your testing?

Testing for issues is a critical part of developing any software, and it’s a meaningful way for anyone to contribute – whether or not you have experience. Details on what to test in WordPress 7.2 are available here.

If you encounter an issue, please share it in the Alpha/Beta area of the support forums. If you are comfortable submitting a reproducible bug report, you can do so via WordPress Trac. You can also check your issue against this list of known bugs.

Curious about testing releases in general and how to get started? Follow along with the testing initiatives in Make Core and join the #core-test channel on Making WordPress Slack.

On October 25, Akismet turns 21. We’re celebrating with a few new guests: an official Drupal module, a PHP SDK, and another year of improvements to our WordPress plugin. Spam still isn’t on the list.

Akismet launched in October 2005 to help people spend less time dealing with comment spam and more time enjoying their blogs. The web has changed a lot since then. People build communities, collect inquiries, accept donations, and create applications on all kinds of platforms. Each of those places gives people a way to contribute. It also gives spammers somewhere to try their luck.

Since then, Akismet has blocked over 570 billion pieces of spam. Every one is something a site owner didn’t have to spend time sorting through. Our birthday wish is to keep making more room for the real people.

Welcome, Drupal

This year, we released the official Akismet Drupal module, built by the team behind Akismet. It brings our spam protection to Drupal comments, contact forms, webforms, and user registrations, with tools for moderators to review submissions and send corrections back to Akismet.

We’ve continued building on that welcome. The latest release supports Drupal 12 and passes richer bot-detection signals into spam scoring. On Drupal 12, comments and registrations are supported now; contact forms, webforms, and the Key module will follow as those modules become ready for Drupal 12.

For people using the older community module, we also built an upgrade path to the official module that carries their API key and protection settings across. The migration guide explains the requirements and which settings need attention.

Welcome, PHP developers

Akismet’s API has long made it possible to protect sites beyond WordPress. This year’s official PHP SDK gives developers a first-party client for bringing that protection into their own PHP applications, including projects built with Laravel or Symfony.

The SDK handles the Akismet API integration so developers can focus on their application. It supports checking submissions, reporting spam and legitimate content, and retrieving usage and account information. The official Drupal module uses it too.

If you’re building a place where people can post, sign up, or send a message, there’s a new tool to help you keep the spam out.

A familiar guest, with a few improvements

WordPress has been with us from the beginning. This year, we kept improving that experience: clearer setup and error messages, accessibility improvements, better detection of automated submissions, and compatibility fixes. You can find the details in the WordPress plugin release log.

Version 5.7 also added support for Abilities and Connectors, helping Akismet fit into WordPress’s evolving tools for integrating external services.

More room for real people

A comment worth replying to. A message from a future customer. A donation to a cause someone cares about. Those are the things we want coming through.

Thank you to everyone who uses Akismet, builds an integration, reports a problem, or helps us improve. You’ve been part of these 21 years, and you’re very much invited to the celebration.

Whether your site runs on WordPress, Drupal, or something you’re building yourself with the PHP SDK, there’s room at the table.

Just no room for spam.

Try out the Drupal module today!

Howdy,

Before anything else: check which version of PHP your sites run. On October 21, the PHP project released fixes for two critical vulnerabilities, and they affect any server running a PHP application, not only WordPress. You’ll find your version under Tools → Site Health → Info → Server in your WordPress admin. If you manage your own server and are still on a version older than 8.2, I highly recommend updating. While many hosts have patched older PHP versions that are end of life, it’s best to stay on versions that PHP officially supports.

On a happier note, I’m back. I was sick for a stretch earlier this month, which is why there was no edition on October 10. Rather than try to cram four weeks into one post, this edition sticks to the last two. Much of what happened in the gap is covered in my October roundup for developers, linked below.

With that, let’s get down to the latest news.

Your friendly neighborhood developer advocate,
Justin Tadlock

Developing Gutenberg and WordPress

The final major release of the year has entered testing. David Baumwald announced that WordPress 7.2 Beta 1 is ready for download and testing, with the final release set for December 8. Notes move into a margin beside the canvas and pick up emoji reactions. Text shadows and form element styling arrive in the design tools, a new Secrets API gives plugins a standard place to store API keys, and client-side media processing extends to the Media Library. There’s even an On This Day dashboard widget. Not everything made it, though: The Repository reports that Notes suggestion mode was punted to 7.3.

The quickest way to try it is the 7.2 Beta 1 Playground instance, or wp core update --version=7.2-beta1 on a test site. Not on production.

Not sure where to start? Noruzzaman’s Help Test WordPress 7.2 breaks the release down by area: security, collaboration, admin, blocks and APIs, design, media. It also walks through the different ways to run a beta, from Playground to a staging site on your host, and points you to where feedback goes. The Beta 1 post is clear that testing counts as contributing, whether or not you’ve done it before.

Your first contribution to WordPress shouldn’t start with installing Git, Node.js, npm, and Docker. That’s the friction the WordPress Contributor Toolkit removes, and Ryan Welcher announced Contributor Toolkit 2.0, a redesigned app in your language. It’s rebuilt on the WordPress Design System, ships in ten languages, and adds a settings dialog. After you apply a patch, you can revert a single file without losing the patch itself. It’s also about 350 MB smaller, which helps when a whole Contributor Day room downloads it at once.

Jorge Costa shared what’s new in Gutenberg 24.2, and the Notes feature is the big headline. Notes now float in a margin the editor reserves next to the canvas, so you no longer have to choose between reading feedback and keeping the Settings sidebar open.

The Navigation block’s link search now looks through pages, posts, categories, and tags at once. Gallery can sort hand-picked images and tint all of them with a single duotone. And the design tools push continues with about 80 more PRs. Minimum width and height controls, for example, went from five blocks to 40.

For developers, React 19 is now on by default. Test your plugins and themes, and if something breaks, you can switch it off under Gutenberg → Experiments. Gutenberg 24.3 RC1 is already out, too, with rich text formatting across blocks, so expect that next week.

On the Developer Blog, I put together What’s new for developers? (October 2026), and I tried something different this month. Instead of walking through every aspect of the project, it focuses on the changes I think matter most if you build on WordPress: custom blocks building their own responsive controls, wp_kses() being rebuilt on the HTML API, stroke-based Core icons, and the automated security review for plugin releases. Everything else is linked at the end.

Readers may remember Chris Zarate’s post on moving collaboration to the server from the last edition. Alec Geatches follows it up with a guide to the sync engines for real-time collaboration, comparing yjs-server, DE-RTC, and intent-log on their strengths and weaknesses. In every engine, each change goes through WordPress, which confirms who sent it, checks their permissions, and validates it before merging. You can try all three in the experimental Gutenberg Sync Engines plugin. It needs WordPress 7.0+ and the Presence API plugin, and it bundles its own copy of Gutenberg, so deactivate the Gutenberg plugin first.

Feature Notifications has been quiet since version 0.2.0 shipped in April 2023. Jonathan Bossenger is reviving it with a status update and plan for 0.3.0, aiming to ship it with WordPress. That would be the project’s first working MVP: a notifications system that creates, stores, displays, and dismisses notifications. His honest assessment is that the foundations are solid but nothing is wired up end to end yet. He’s posting weekly updates if you want to follow along or help.

Benjamin Zekavica published the recap of the WordPress 7.1 “Mary Lou” retrospective, summarizing what contributors would keep, add, and change for future release squads. If you answered the survey, this is where your feedback landed.

Plugins, Themes, and Tools for #nocode site builders and owners

Sticky headers are one of those things you end up fixing on nearly every block theme site. Jamie Marsland turned his fix into a free plugin, Jamie’s Header Effects.

The standout is Chameleon mode: as visitors scroll, the header picks up the background color of the section beneath it and flips its text between light and dark to stay readable. There are also frosted-glass, solid, hide-on-scroll, and transparent overlay styles. It finds your header template part on its own, respects prefers-reduced-motion, and lives under Appearance → Header Effects.

Meta Box’s custom models no longer have to sit in isolation. A few weeks after moving model creation into the builder, Lua Nguyen announced the new Custom Model field, which lets you pick one or more items from a custom model the same way the Post field picks posts. MB Relationships also gains a Model object type, so you can connect models to posts, terms, users, or other models in either direction. Think hotel rooms as a post type with bookings attached from a custom model—no IDs stored by hand.

On WordPress.com, Ronnie Burt covers what’s new with WordPress Agent: it now designs a custom theme from your answers, hands you off to a simplified AI Editor with Preview and Edit tabs, and can install and manage plugins when you ask. The latest WordPress.com changelog also opens premium themes to every paid plan, starting with Personal.

WooCommerce 11.2.1 fixes two regressions: classic checkout on stores that remove address fields with filters, and postcode validation in the Checkout block for Argentina and a few other countries.

Theme Development for Full Site Editing and Blocks

If you’ve ever had to explain to a client why they should move to a block theme, Simon Cooke has done the work for you. His Human Made guide on how a WordPress block theme is built, and why it matters for enterprise sites walks through each part of a block theme and who owns it, with a side-by-side comparison to classic themes. He’s clear that moving is a project, not a theme swap. The point he lands on: when design rules live in the theme, a page built by someone who joined last week follows the same rules as one the designer built.

What if you could point a tool at any static HTML and CSS site and get an editable block theme back, headers and footers included? That’s the Static Site Importer, and Chris Huber of Automattic talks it through with Nathan Wrigley on WP Tavern in episode #238 on making migration to WordPress easier than ever. You’ll hear how it crawls a site, maps HTML elements to blocks, and handles trickier features like WooCommerce, plus how it fits into the broader Data Liberation effort.

WooCommerce’s Purple theme has a new home. Luigi Teschio announced that Purple development moves to the WooCommerce monorepo, as the first theme in its new themes/ directory, so contributions and bug reports go there now. One of the stated reasons is that keeping themes next to the blocks they use makes it easier for contributors, and AI coding tools, to see how templates and patterns use WooCommerce blocks. Nothing changes for existing installs, and Purple still releases on its own schedule. For more background, Bob Dunn’s Do the Woo episode on WooCommerce themes in 2026 covers Purple and theme performance.

Building Blocks and Tools for the Block editor.

The new @wordpress/ui package will gradually replace @wordpress/components, so how much of an existing plugin can you move over today? Ryan Welcher found out live by migrating Advanced Query Loop to @wordpress/ui with the Design System MCP.

Once your page registers WebMCP tools, those tool definitions are an API, and the consumer is a language model. Pascal Birchler built playwright-webmcp for testing WebMCP tool surfaces, with linting, Playwright matchers, agent evals, and a site audit CLI. He lists the failure modes that make this tricky: vague descriptions the model ignores, schemas the browser quietly rejects, and two tools on the same page with nearly identical names.

Extension developers no longer need to duplicate a WooCommerce ability just to expose a few extra fields. Luis Felipe Zaguini opened a call for testing extensible abilities for extension fields, an experimental API in WooCommerce 11.3. Extensions can add fields to product, order, and order item reads and writes, register query filters, and refuse a change with a validator before it saves. It’s off by default, so turn on Extensible abilities under WooCommerce → Settings → Advanced → Features to try it. The gift wrap example in the post is a good place to start.

What’s new in Playground?

The best way to find out what’s hard about site editing is to watch someone try it. Jamie Marsland built a user testing app for WordPress on Playground and Spacefast to do exactly that. You send a tester a link, and Playground spins up a fresh site in their browser from your existing demo blueprint, with a card of five to seven tasks in the corner. The results page shows how long each task took, who needed the hint, and whether the site actually changed. It’s also an MCP server, and it’ll flag a task that gives away the button name.

AI in WordPress

Two weeks after the MCP Adapter arrived on WordPress.org as a canonical plugin, the AI team got approval to make MCP a default part of WordPress. Rae Morey reports on the move to make MCP a default part of WordPress, with 7.3 floated as a target. That doesn’t necessarily mean merging the adapter into Core: bundling it, enabling it through existing interfaces, and building specific capabilities into Core are all on the table. It’s also a reversal of the reasoning behind the canonical plugin, and maintainers are asking what changed. The AI contributor summary for October 21 has the meeting’s side of the discussion.

Andy Peatling launched WordPress Agent Benchmarks to measure how AI agents handle WordPress, and Rae Morey walks through the first results. Across 193 sites built for requests that suited WordPress, agents chose it zero times, even though they named it as an option about half the time. Using the MCP Adapter alone, they completed no tasks on existing sites, largely because it doesn’t yet bundle the abilities for common operations. Brian Coords asks what WordPress would have to change in helping agents choose WordPress, drawing on a WP Minute panel with Andy.

Is the MCP Adapter safe? Brad Williams of WebDevStudios calls it a door: “You decide which rooms it opens into.” He explains why production use of the MCP Adapter is a governance decision, not a plugin decision. An agent gets whatever abilities are exposed, using the permissions of the user it connects as, and every plugin you install can add more. His advice is to write the agent’s job description before you hand over the keys.

If you connect an AI client to WooCommerce, this one needs action before you upgrade. Darren Ethier explains that WooCommerce 11.3 removes its deprecated MCP endpoint. Requests to /wp-json/woocommerce/mcp will return a 410. Install the MCP Adapter, create an application password for a user with only the capabilities the client needs, and point the client at the adapter’s default server. Extensions that hooked into the old endpoint’s filters should check the post’s full list of what’s been removed.

WPShout’s guide on how to connect Claude to WordPress opens with the question most guides skip: where your site is hosted decides which route you take. WordPress.com, Jetpack, and other self-hosted sites each get their own path, and the walkthrough uses a free MCP plugin with a least-privilege grant. It’s also candid about a gap: the WordPress MCP Adapter has no OAuth server of its own, so claude.ai’s sign-in can’t connect to it directly yet.

Post revisions spent years bloating databases. Human Made thinks they’re about to become valuable. In WordPress revisions: agentic gold?, Noel argues that every revision records what changed, who changed it, and when, which makes them a log of how your team really works. Mine them for repeated changes and you’ve found the workflows an agent could take over. The post includes a prompt you can run, on a copy of your database and never on production.

Need a plugin .zip from Gutenberg’s master branch?
Gutenberg Times provides daily build for testing and review.

Now also available via WordPress Playground. There is no need for a test site locally or on a server. Have you been using it? Email me with your experience.

The PHP project has announced a security release that fixes two critical security vulnerabilities discovered in PHP.

Due to the critical severity of the issues, site owners are encouraged to immediately update their installations of PHP. Your web host may already be working to update PHP and put web application firewall (WAF) rules in place to mitigate the vulnerabilities, but you should still check for updates from your web host and, if necessary, update PHP as soon as possible.

Within WordPress, you can see which version of PHP your site runs under Tools > Site Health > Info > Server. Many web hosts provide this information in your web hosting administration panel too.

These vulnerabilities are not specific to WordPress and affect any server that hosts a PHP application. No WordPress update is required or planned for these issues.

Versions of PHP prior to 8.2 no longer receive security updates from the PHP project.

If your site runs a version prior to this and you manage your own web hosting, you should consider taking your server offline while you prepare to update to a newer version of PHP. This advice is being published by several national cyber security agencies. To quote the UK National Cyber Security Centre:

Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.

Further information on wordpress.org:

  • Get a faster, more secure website: update PHP today
  • PHP Compatibility and WordPress Versions
  • FAQ My site was hacked

Jukebox is a podcast which is dedicated to all things WordPress. The people, the events, the plugins, the blocks, the themes, and in this case, how the Static Site Importer makes migrating any website to WordPress easier than ever.

If you’d like to subscribe to the podcast, you can do that by searching for WP Tavern in your podcast player of choice, or by going to wptavern.com/feed/podcast, and you can copy that URL into most podcast players.

So on the podcast today we have Chris Huber. Chris’s journey with WordPress began in his college days, first as a writer and blogger, and eventually progressing to software engineering after moving his personal site, extrachill.com to WordPress in 2018, Chris went deeply into WordPress, developing custom plugins and exploring all the corners of the platform. His passion for experimentation and creative tech led him to Automattic where he now helps shape the WordPress experience as a software engineer.

Our discussion centres around two main topics, Data Liberation and the Static Site Importer tool.

We focus upon the evolving landscape of website migration and ownership. Chris explains how Data Liberation aims to make it easier for users to take control of their sites, whether they’re moving to WordPress from platforms like Wix, Squarespace, or Drupal, or just want portability for their data.

We also get into the Static Site Importer, which takes this a step further by converting any static HTML / CSS website into a fully editable WordPress block theme, headers, footers, and all.

Chris walks us through how these tools work in tandem, highlighting the mechanics behind website crawling, mapping HTML elements to Gutenberg blocks, and handling complex features like WooCommerce and calendars.

We talk about the continuous improvement of these tools, how each migration helps raise the bar for future imports, and how this project could fundamentally change the way people move websites between platforms.

If you’re curious about the future of website migration, and how WordPress is removing the hurdles for users who want to truly own and manage their content, this episode is for you.

On the podcast today we have Chris Huber.

Chris’s journey with WordPress began back in his college days, first as a writer and blogger and eventually progressing to software engineering. After moving his personal site, extrachill.com, to WordPress in 2018, Chris went deeply into WordPress, developing custom plugins and exploring all the corners of the platform. His passion for experimentation and creative tech led him to Automattic, where he now helps shape the WordPress experience as a software engineer.

Our discussion centers around two main topics: Data Liberation and the Static Site Importer tool. We focused upon the evolving landscape of website migration and ownership. Chris explains how Data Liberation aims to make it easier for users to take control of their site, whether they’re moving to WordPress from platforms like Wix, Squarespace, or Drupal, or just want portability for their data.

We also get into the Static Site Importer, which takes this a step further by converting any static HTML / CSS website into a fully editable WordPress block theme, headers, footers, and all.

Chris walks us through how these tools work in tandem, highlighting the mechanics behind website crawling, mapping HTML elements to Gutenberg blocks, and handling complex features like WooCommerce and calendars.

We talk about the continuous improvement of these tools, how each migration helps raise the bar for future imports, and how this project could fundamentally change the way people move websites between platforms.

If you’re curious about the future of website migration and how WordPress is removing the hurdles for users who want to truly own and manage their content, this episode is for you.

Editing Experience

Responsive Design Controls

Building on the responsive design improvements introduced in WordPress 7.1, WordPress 7.2 expands viewport-specific styling to additional design tools and blocks. Creators gain more granular control over how layouts and visual settings adapt across screen sizes, including responsive Gallery settings for columns, image cropping, and aspect ratios.

Learn more: GitHub #80388, #82003

Improved Global Styles and Design Tools

WordPress 7.2 makes site-wide styling easier to manage with a new Customized filter for finding blocks with modified styles and inherited Global Styles values displayed directly in block inspector controls. Expanded design tools and support for styling form elements provide additional flexibility when creating a consistent visual identity across a site.

Learn more: GitHub #82520, #76525, #34198, #84657

Text Shadow Support

WordPress 7.2 introduces new text shadow controls, giving creators more ways to add depth and emphasis to their content. Text shadows can be customized through block settings and defined as presets in theme.json, making it easier to maintain consistent typography across a site.

Learn more: GitHub #73320, GitHub #79584, Trac #65869

Easier Navigation Management

Improvements to the Site Editor make managing navigation links more intuitive. Creators can add, organize, and edit navigation items directly from the editor sidebar, making it easier to maintain site menus without interrupting their editing workflow.

Learn more: GitHub #77069

Better Collaboration with Notes

WordPress 7.2 introduces Emoji reactions on notes and a new toolbar icon that makes Notes easier to access and manage. Notes move to the editor canvas, bringing conversations directly into the margin. Users can now keep Notes and the block settings sidebar open simultaneously, making it easier to review feedback while editing content.

A new minimized Notes mode reduces visual clutter, while improvements to positioning and display create a smoother, more consistent collaboration experience.

Learn more: GitHub #79970, GitHub #83786, GitHub #80015, Trac #64638

Faster, More Efficient Media Uploads

WordPress 7.2 expands client-side media processing to the Media Library, allowing images to be resized, compressed, and converted directly in the browser before being uploaded. This can improve upload performance, reduce server resource usage, and provide better support for modern image formats, particularly on hosting environments with limited image-processing capabilities.

Learn more: Trac #65661, GitHub #12585

New “On This Day” Dashboard Widget

WordPress 7.2 introduces a new On This Day dashboard widget that helps users rediscover content published on the same date in previous years. By highlighting posts from the site’s history, the widget makes it easier to revisit past content, celebrate milestones, and find opportunities to refresh or reshare older posts.

Learn more: Trac #65116

Block Editor Usability Improvements

WordPress 7.2 includes a collection of smaller improvements aimed at reducing friction in everyday editing. These changes include clearer error messages, more helpful feedback when something goes wrong, and refinements to common editor interactions, making the editing experience more predictable and approachable.

Learn more: GitHub #81453, #82496, #84656, #84649

A More Consistent WordPress Admin

WordPress 7.2 continues modernizing the administration experience by replacing legacy Dashicons in the admin bar and sidebar with icons from the WordPress icon library. The updated icons bring greater visual consistency between the traditional WordPress dashboard and newer editing interfaces.

Learn more: GitHub #12270

An Updated Block Settings Experience

A new DataForm-powered inspector introduces a refreshed approach to managing block settings in the editor. Built on the DataForm component system, this work aims to provide more consistent controls and a more extensible foundation for future block editing improvements.

Learn more: GitHub Gutenberg · Call for Testing

Faster WordPress Administration

WordPress 7.2 improves admin performance by modernizing how scripts and stylesheets are loaded. Instead of combining assets into large files, WordPress now loads them individually for better browser caching. A new prefetching mechanism also anticipates which admin screen users are likely to visit next, loading its resources in advance to make navigation between the dashboard, post lists, and editor faster.

Learn more: Trac #57548

For Developers

New Secrets API

WordPress 7.2 introduces a Secrets API, providing developers with a standardized, secure way to store sensitive credentials such as API keys and authentication tokens. The API supports encryption at rest, credential rotation, and customizable storage providers, helping plugins and integrations manage sensitive information more securely.

Learn more (Trac #66187)

Random Content Redirects

WordPress 7.2 adds support for random content redirects, allowing visitors to discover a randomly selected post through a dedicated URL. This provides a simple way to encourage content exploration and help readers rediscover older posts.

Learn more: Trac #64498

More Powerful APIs for Developers

WordPress 7.2 expands the Abilities API with new capabilities for accessing and querying WordPress data, providing a more consistent foundation for integrations, automation, and AI-powered tools. (Trac #66268, #64605, #64657)

Enhancements to the Interactivity API introduce new ways to render trusted HTML and manage reactive navigation, giving developers more flexibility when building dynamic, interactive blocks. (Trac #66246, Gutenberg PR #83092)

Additional improvements to the HTML API, block supports, and responsive design tools provide more reliable markup processing and greater control over how custom blocks are styled and displayed across devices. (Trac #65824, #66150, #65869)

How important is your testing?

Testing for issues is a critical part of developing any software, and it’s a meaningful way for anyone to contribute – whether or not you have experience. Details on what to test in WordPress 7.2 are available here.

If you encounter an issue, please share it in the Alpha/Beta area of the support forums. If you are comfortable submitting a reproducible bug report, you can do so via WordPress Trac. You can also check your issue against this list of known bugs.

Curious about testing releases in general and how to get started? Follow along with the testing initiatives in Make Core and join the #core-test channel on Making WordPress Slack.

WordPress 7.2 will include new features that were previously only available in the Gutenberg plugin. Learn more about Gutenberg updates since WordPress 7.1 in the What’s New in Gutenberg posts for versions 23.7, 23.8, 23.9, 24.0, 24.1, 24.2, and 24.3.

What’s new in WordPress 7.2?

With so much in progress for WordPress 7.2 Beta 1, this is still only the beginning; expect continued refinement with each Beta and RC release ahead of the final release on December 8, 2026

Secrets bloom, designs take shape
New blocks come alive

OpenStation is a free WordPress plugin that turns wp-admin into a desktop. Every admin screen opens in its own window that you can move, resize and keep open next to the others. You can try it in your browser right now, with nothing to install.

Can’t see the video? Watch it on YouTube.

Why we built it

Most of us spend the day jumping between screens in wp-admin. You open a post, go back to the list, check the media library, then go back again. With OpenStation, those screens stay open side by side, so you don’t lose your place.

What you get

  • A window for every admin page: posts, media, settings, plugins
  • A dock with your whole admin menu, including your other plugins
  • Several desktops, for example one for writing and one for site settings
  • Wallpapers, widgets and accent colors
  • Cmd+K to jump anywhere fast
  • Your windows are still open when you come back

Try it in your browser

Go to the OpenStation page on WordPress.org and click Live Preview. It runs a full WordPress site with OpenStation in your browser tab, so you can’t break anything.

Install it on your site

  1. In your admin, go to Plugins → Add New and search for “OpenStation”
  2. Click Install Now, then Activate
  3. Click the desktop icon in the top-right corner of the admin bar

It’s safe to try

OpenStation is opt-in for each user, so the rest of your team keeps the normal admin. Click the same icon to go back to the classic view. If you deactivate the plugin, wp-admin goes back to exactly how it was. It doesn’t change WordPress core.

Tell us what you think

Have a question? Ask in the support forum. Found a bug or have an idea? Open an issue on GitHub.
