I made a WordPress plugin for my holidays. It’s called Travel Steps, and it turns a trip into a page with a map down one side and the story of each day down the other.

Every photo I take ends up in Immich, on my own server. My phone sends where I’ve been to Dawarich, on the same server. So after a trip I have all the photos and the whole route, sitting in two apps on my private server. The travel apps that make nice trip pages want your photos and your location on their servers. I’d rather keep them on mine.

How it works

You make a trip, give it a first and last day, and press Sync. Travel Steps asks Dawarich for your location over those days, and Immich for the photos you took. You can pick one Immich album instead. If you don’t use Immich at all, upload the photos to the trip. It will detect the start and end dates from the uploaded photos, or an Immich album too.

Sync makes a draft post for every day that has favourite photos. Each one is a “step”. It splits the day into places too. A new place starts when a favourite is more than 2 km from the last one and in a different town. Each place gets a heading and a block of photos, so all that’s left is the writing.

Place names come from GeoNames data that ships with the plugin, so naming a town doesn’t send your location anywhere. Immich only names a place from a photo’s own GPS. A photo from a camera without GPS gets placed from your Dawarich history instead, and named the same way.

Publish the days you want people to see. Drafts stay private, and so do their photos.

The distance at the top follows the whole route, flights included. GPS glitches that put you in the Atlantic for a second are dropped. Anything you’d have needed to travel faster than 1,080 km/h to reach counts as a glitch. Sorry, Concorde.

Your photos stay at home

Visitors never talk to Immich. WordPress fetches each photo, caches it and serves it itself, so Immich and the original files stay private. It caches a trip’s photos in the background after a sync. The trip keeps working when Immich is down. A daily sweep deletes cached photos older than a number of days you choose, whether a trip still uses them or not, and they’re fetched again the next time someone looks.

Photos you upload to a trip keep their GPS in the original, but it’s stripped from every copy WordPress makes, and only those copies are ever sent. A trip can have a password, and you can let some logged-in people skip it.

Pin, hide, cover

Hover over a photo to pin it (always show it), hide it, or make it the trip’s cover. The rest of the day’s photos sit behind a “Show more photos” link.

On phones, those buttons show up after you press Edit photos as illustrated by the images below.

Tap a photo and it opens full screen. On a phone you swipe from one photo to the next, edge to edge. On a desktop there are arrows, and the arrow keys work too.

Try it

Here’s a demo in WordPress Playground. It’s a week in the west of Ireland, running in your browser that installs nothing. Stand-in Immich and Dawarich servers feed the real sync code with photos from Unsplash. You’re logged in as an admin, so press Sync, pin and hide photos, and edit the days in the block editor. It all disappears when you close the tab.

The code is on GitHub. To install it, download travel-steps.zip from the latest release and upload it under Plugins → Add New. It needs WordPress 6.7 and PHP 8.0. Immich and Dawarich are both optional. It has been submitted to WordPress.org but if you read this blog, you’ll know how to install a plugin from a zip file!

WpApp

Travel Steps is built on WpApp, Alex Kirk’s framework for building apps on top of WordPress.

A plugin usually adds screens to wp-admin, or puts its pages inside your theme and hopes the CSS gets along. A WpApp app gets its own URLs instead (/travel-steps/ here), and its pages are plain HTML with no theme in the way. WordPress still does the boring work: users and logins, roles, the block editor, the REST API, cron and the database. WpApp adds the bits in between:

  • URL routing, using WordPress rewrite rules,
  • pages that don’t load your theme,
  • the admin bar on every page, with the app’s own icon (the green map at the top of my screenshots),
  • access control using WordPress capabilities.

You can start one with composer create-project akirk/create-wp-app my-app. Alex has a showcase of apps built with it, including a cookbook and a family wiki.

Built with Claude Code

I wrote Travel Steps with Claude Code. The first commit was on 11 October, and there are many more now. Most of the work went round the same loop. I file an issue, Claude fixes it test-first on a branch and opens a pull request, and other agents review it. I deploy it to my own server and try it. The tests run in WordPress Playground too, the same as the demo.

If you run Immich, give it a whirl. Bug reports welcome on GitHub

In mid-April 2026 my employer started a project called “Radical Speed Month” to step away from our existing structures and processes, make space for people to dive more deeply into AI tooling, and try to build new or sleeping ideas. My participation in this experiment ran until late September and I stacked up a lot of explorations without having written about them or about the process. In this post I’d like to highlight some of the results of this time and share some learnings.

Selected lessons

  • Massive agentic deployment demands heavy storage and generic compute capacity — inference is not the only bottleneck. This is necessary to support massively parallel checkouts of code, benchmarking, analysis of other software and data, running hierarchies of thousands of test workers and headless browsers, generating and analyzing image and video artifacts, creating indexes, and more.
  • Instructing an agent to “find the five hidden defects” is more effective at finding real issues than asking if there are any hidden defects. They may return false claims, but they try to answer the questions they are prompted — it’s not that different than the comparison between asking someone what in their day brought them a smile, or what was difficult for them, rather than asking “how was your day?”
  • Agents with web searching capabilities are powerful knowledge-retrieval and aggregation tools. Reports they generate to aid in developing code can be more effective than asking the agents to generate the code directly.
  • Models today are incredibly powerful, but guiding human insight is also powerful. Autonomous agentic activity demonstrated a tendency to produce more evidence of accomplished work than actual accomplished work. In a strange way this might reflect the training dataset: corporations must also guard against the dangers of overly-burdensome paperwork.

Projects

All of the projects here were almost entirely built by AI agents, but with my guidance and supervision. Therefore, credit for each of them does not rest entirely with me. However, for the sake of brevity I will omit mentioning in each one that AI tooling was the actual producer.

Each project below is assigned a truly unscientific evaluation:

  • The project succeeded with clear value.
  • The project completed its goals, but the value is unclear.
  • The hard work has completed, but I need to close the loop and deploy it.
  • The idea is sound but not ready; it needs more development.
  • The project failed to bear fruit for any reason.

My personal favorites:

  • Fix bugs in proprietary hardware drivers
  • Gather empirical evidence to guide development decisions
  • Stream real-world HTML from Common Crawl
  • Provide deep insight into PHP script execution
  • Rapidly prototype a comprehensive collaborative editing environment for WordPress

Tools

Because I expected a short availability for the enhanced AI access, I prioritized building, early on, tools whose value would outlast the project. Generally I prefer working in offline or local environments, so I built archivers for several services which are only available when connected to the Internet.

While MCP servers were very popular at this time, I have always been unhappy with the load centralization and amplification they create. The same is true for any online resource against which agents perform searches. My intuition is that it’s more considerate to those services to make one batched update, to download all new data since the last sync, than it is to make repeated queries which might overwhelm their servers and fetch the same resources over and over.

Being offline and local, the archivers are extremely fast and operate in the terminal where I prefer to interact.

GitHub archive

Finding GitHub’s search functionality lacking, and wishing for a chronological stream of my activity, I built github-archiver so I could have the tools and performance I wanted. This initially supported searching through PRs, issues, and comments, as well as rendering my own activity in a reverse-chronological view. I eventually added two additional views for replies: people I replied to, and people who had replied to me. This gives me great awareness of my recent conversations and has helped me to avoid losing conversations. Sometimes I struggle to find a PR that I meant to follow-up on, but it disappears from my GitHub notifications and I can’t remember the exact wording that will turn it up in a search result. I even tend to forget in which code repository it was left, so my tool aggregates activity across all archived repositories.

The basic design is a compressed HTTP cache of the GitHub API. When fetching or updating, it respects rate limits and leans on HTTP headers to avoid wasted transfers. After some work with banking APIs several years ago, I found that storing raw HTTP responses proved more flexible than parsing into a custom internal data type, as it lets me rewrite logic in the app later without having to re-download the entire archive. This came in handy several times as I expanded the search index and added more functionality.

The tool renders GitHub content as richly-formatted and highlighted text in a console unless running outside of an interactive TTY. It renders Markdown and HTML content into this rich text format and lays out meta elements in a meaningful way. Its speed, zero-network dependence, and minimized output make it a good fit for agents that would otherwise be hammering GitHub’s API, waiting, and wasting tokens on irrelevant content.

Trac archive

Just like the github-archiver, I built a trac-archive for WordPress’ Trac system. It is feature-similar to the GitHub archiver, but provides an additional perk: because bots relay messages from GitHub back into Trac, issues often have two markup formats in use simultaneously. My trac-archive first parses its content according to Trac’s own system, but then it additionally parses Markdown where it finds it. It shares much of the rendering logic with the github-archiver and provides a clearer experience than the web view due to the additional parsing, syntax highlighting, and ability to exclude bot traffic from the results.

Review the evolution of a series of commits over time

git-sequence-patch was used to help me understand the full scope of the WordPress collaborative editor project. Since many large features or projects span many commits and possibly even months or years of work, this tool reads a number of git commit SHAs and will build a fictitious patch that more or less represents how the entire project would be proposed were it to be proposed against the latest branch head. Another way to look at this is to generate one massive revert commit for the original feature and all descendant changes to it since its inception.

This is a project I had been wanting to build for a long time; for each of the given commits, it tracks which lines were changed by the commits, and then steps forward through the branch history, noting when other commits also modify or remove those lines. Once it completes at the branch head, it prepares a patch to replace all of those lines with the code that was there before the original patch, and reverse the patch. This means that it doesn’t produce a patch that would actually merge, but it produces a patch that’s useful for understanding the full scope of how a change evolves over time.

It’s line-oriented and so would miss some obvious scope. For example, if tracing the sequence for a new function, it will miss a later change which calls into that function. This would actually be possible to add to the tool as an enhancement, but it wasn’t necessary for my purposes at the time and I think it would remain ideally an option rather than a default behavior.

I spend a lot of time trying to quickly understand entire systems that I didn’t write or have any experience with, and this tool is a delight for answering the question: “how has this change evolved through time?”

Analyze real-world HTML from Common Crawl

To better test the HTML API against real HTML documents, I built cc-analyzer, which feeds data from the Common Crawl index into a user-supplied PHP script. This operates in two modes: streaming and batched. In streaming mode it continuously sends HTML documents from the archive into the analysis script. In batched mode, it saves documents from the archive into a subdirectory and then may be invoked again to re-run those documents through specific analysis scripts.

This project has greatly benefited the testing and verification of the HTML API, and informed decisions about what actual HTML syntax patterns exist on the web and what concerns are practical and which are esoteric. Throughout this grand experiment I have examined hundreds of thousands of HTML documents to test the HTML API code, to understand reported and actual text encodings of websites at large, to benchmark changes and optimizations for the HTML API, and to understand parsing needs of real HTML documents.

Instantly search code from the WordPress ecosystem

Veloria.dev (formerly WPDirectory.net) provides fast code search across all of the plugins and themes listed on the WordPress directory. It was experiencing elevated outage rates and I decided at the start of September to recreate it locally as a single binary with a simple compressed offline archive. Previous efforts to slurp the directory left efficiency gains on the table and output around 120 GB of data on the filesystem. By taking advantage of available concurrency, streaming computation as resources are downloaded, pruning the stored files to those which were being indexed, and saving into a custom compressed binary object, my wp-code-search tool was able to archive the directory in five hours storing only 5 GB among three data files: a compressed archive of the source files, a search index, and a metadata archive.

This idea originally came from Dan Luu, who commented that “if we’re repeatedly searching for text on a computer, the obvious thing to do to speed that up isn’t to write a native code compiler for regex matching, it’s to create an index.” Code searches across the entire directory typically return within 10 ms, output syntax-highlighted snippets from the files in which they are found, and the tool can extract those files or entire plugins from the compressed archive. The index is sorted by active installs so the most-deployed results appear first.

This tool has become an invaluable daily driver for me as I refactor Core WordPress internals and want to avoid needlessly breaking existing code.

Towards the end of September I had another long-shot idea: could the ideas making the text search so fast be mixed with structural queries so that I could perform data-flow and control-flow analysis on the code? Turns out that yes, with another 5 GB sidecar index, and a custom WordPress-specific query syntax this was not only possible, but practical with many complicated queries executing in anywhere from a few seconds to a few tens of seconds.

There’s a lot of power in this query syntax to identify complicated code structures and I still have to learn how to generate the kinds of queries I want to. I built the structural code search to aid in discovery of risky code patterns to harden as part of my work improving WordPress’ security stance.

Text-mode access to the modern web

My zs tool performs web searches and downloads rendered HTML pages in the terminal. Fascinatingly enough, when I attempted to start this project I tried explaining very clearly that I wanted to adhere to the terms of use for all services, that I wanted to respect the remote servers providing the content, and that this was a user-agent acting on my behalf to perform queries in the terminal instead of a browser. Unfortunately, it seems like the instructions to follow the rules were misinterpreted as attempted bypasses and overly-refused.

Regardless, I was able to create this non-GUI browser and build up enough of the Web Platform to render the pages I wanted to view. When Captchas and other verification interstitials appear, they render inline into the terminal via terminal raster commands. I’m able to indicate which boxes contain the bus, or motorcycle, or a bridge, which Google seems really intent on learning, and continue with text flows and shell pipelines.

My motivation for building this was to perform web searches from the CLI, but once I had the mechanisms in place to interact with the search engines, I realized I could also use this to grab dynamically-rendered pages. For any given URL, a page loads, executes scripts, and renders until the JavaScript event queue empties or a timeout trips, and then the final DOM serializes into the HTML output.

This makes the tool more valuable than my typical curl flow, which too-often downloads an empty HTML page reminding me that I should be using JavaScript. Because it implemented so much of a browser’s internals, I added a feature to extract the visible text content of the rendered page, something which is surprisingly difficult to download without a full browser and CSS engine, and something which is really valuable when trying to pipe documentation pages into coding agents.

All in all it’s a bit buggy and I would like to start over based on what I learned along the way. It still works sometimes and it’s valuable to me when web pages return otherwise-empty mountains of script contents.

WordPress.com

Clarify wording in notification messages

WordPress.com sends notifications about comments, likes, follows, etc., and sometimes the wording is awkward or inconsistent. I generated a report classifying emotional content of the wording and suggested improvements to better inform the reader of what they could or needed to do. It was effective at joining snippets of strings that are concatenated together throughout the code and provided useful insights. It also provided good suggestions for updates that focused on removing anxiety and clarifying possible actions to take in response to the alerts (e.g. replace “Renewal Failed” with “Payment did not go through; update by May 18 to keep your plan active”). Unfortunately those updates are still on my backlog to deploy.

Migrate confused legacy data to simplify runtime code

There are old notification records in the database with conflated and truncated values, and these require complicated code when rendering them to make sense of the confused properties. I was hoping that it would be possible to have the AI examine these broken records and the generating code and provide clear guidance on how to update them. Among 3,000 old records in the database, it proposed seventeen cases for recovery and fixing. Unfortunately this also sits in my backlog to assess and apply.

Fix translation issues and typos

Developers frequently concatenate separately-translated strings which lead to confusing translations. I ran an analysis for this kind of translation issue inside the notifications source code and also for typos and other mistakes. This produced a list of around fifty bug-fixes, including for a missing namespace specifier that was broken for more than a decade and which hadn’t been noticed in error logs, malformed HTML tags which had been hard-coded in string literals, plenty of concatenated translated strings, broken interpolation placeholders, missing calls to the translation function, and missing null checks. This was deployed in May to the production system.

WordPress, the open-source project

Generate automatic previews for dev-docs changes

WordPress Playground runs a copy of PHP and WordPress entirely in the browser via compilation into a WASM environment. It provides testable previews for WordPress and Gutenberg PRs. Missing has been a way to preview changes to the generated developer documentation, which is notoriously difficult to get running at all, let alone dynamically in a browser. I proposed a demonstrator in #29 that does just that through a GitHub Actions workflow on PRs. It has inspired follow-up, but due to the need to ensure a maintainable solution, is still pending deployment.

Harmonize the ignore ruleset across git and Subversion

The official WordPress source code lives in Subversion with a git mirror. The .gitignore and Subversion ignore rulesets are fundamentally distinct from each other, notably in that git ignore patterns apply recursively through a file tree. I attempted to use AI to harmonize the rulesets. Some adjustments were made, but the entire set still needs careful review.

Visualize per-package activity within Gutenberg

To better understand per-package activity within the Gutenberg editor project, I produced a visualization showing commit activity.

Provide deep insight into PHP script execution

Inspired by my childhood Gameshark, I built a PHP extension to improve my ability to debug and analyze PHP script runs. This started as a way to compare two runs of a given script, but expanded into a set of related but distinct modes.

Differential mode compares which functions were called and how many times across two different script runs; this could be useful for performance optimizations or comparing what runs for two different code paths and was built initially while working on page renders vs API call responses.

Trace value records every function or method call whose arguments contain a requested value. It tracks user space as well as builtin functions and was built to help identify code paths which send untransformed data where it shouldn’t reach. A follow transformations option tracks not only the given value, but also common escaped, encoded, serialized, quoted, slashed, and other variations of it. This is a clever security tool for finding out where and how unwanted data is passed around.

Invariant mode takes a PHP file with “hooks” that attach to functions and methods, either during entry into those contexts or when returning from them. They are supplied the values to the arguments, the $this value if a method, and the return value if a post hook. This enables a novel approach to applying software contracts on code with neither the production runtime overhead nor the noise from the contract-enforcement. This was loosely inspired by Clojure’s core.spec. Because the hooks file is user-space PHP code with access to global state, this provides mechanisms for enhanced testing and analysis code, and when registering a shutdown handler in PHP, can print reports at the end of script execution. Hooks may also raise exceptions to halt execution when any desired invariant is violated, such as when preg_match() receives a pattern that might be attempting to parse HTML.

Unused runtime coverage mode generates a report of all loaded identifiers which were never read or executed during a script execution. A sampling option can be used in production to assemble such a report, probabilistically, over time. This mode was designed to find effectively dead-code that might be lurking behind runtime conditions which can never actually run due to real data distributions. For example, a function which is only ever called before a given date, when the given date is several years in the past. Static analysis will miss this while a month of production sampling with no calls will provide evidence that it’s safe to remove the function, that no other strange or unexpected call-paths are still calling it.

Trace allocations mode traces heap allocations made by PHP during a script execution. It immediately surfaced unnecessary allocation in wp_is_numeric_array(), which was promptly eliminated in [#12100].

This extension has provided incredible insight into how WordPress and other PHP scripts run, and I’ve only scratched the surface of how I can take advantage of it.

Introduce dynamic security policies into PHP with eBPF to isolate plugin code and extensions

Like the php-gameshark extension, I built a modified php binary which coordinates with eBPF in the Linux kernel to apply dynamic security policies and create isolated security domains within executing PHP code. There is no logical separation between executing the Core WordPress code and the code from plugins running on a site. This is a security challenge because the two kinds of code warrant different trust, and a site operator may want to assign unique trust and capabilities to different plugins.

This extension provides a wp_runtime_security_apply_policies() function which registers sandboxing rules against files whose source code matches the provided glob. It allows disabling network access, shell execution, sending of emails, reading uploaded files, and writing uploaded files demonstrating a path towards securing WordPress sites from errant or malicious plugins, as well as an explicit opt-in capability model for plugins as they have need. It doesn’t just protect user-space PHP code either; thanks to the fact that policy enforcement occurs within eBPF, it can also apply the same policies against compiled PHP extensions running on the host, assuming that the extensions are not actively attempting to exploit the guards (the protection is aimed at security vulnerabilities within the commonly-deployed PHP extensions, not against potentially-malicious extensions).

I built this extension after a discussion with Lynn Griffith at WordCamp US in late August. It seems promising but is under-developed and needs production testing. As it relies on eBPF, it only supports Linux environments, ruling out Windows, BSD, and macOS-based hosts.

Benchmark HTML parsing optimizations against realistic data from the Internet

With the aid of cc-analyzer, I automated the benchmarking of numerous optimizations that we have explored over the years with the HTML API, mostly changes to the internal data structures and how attributes are represented during the parse. The AI tooling provided the run-scripts for cc-analyzer, invoked it, and gathered the results. It also collected PRs that I had proposed (using the github-archiver) since May 2023 so that I didn’t have to find them.

Fuzz-test the HTML API

I fuzz-tested the HTML API, finding several unreported bugs, including easy-to-overlook defects in the code. Fuzzing in this way also prevented a number of defects with the rewrite of wp_kses(). This complements the existing spec-compliance tests against the html5lib test suite, practical tests against real HTML from the web, and a unit-test suite covering intentional behaviors.

Scaffold fuzz-testing in Gutenberg

I attempted to build a generalizable fuzz-testing infrastructure for the Gutenberg editor. This was an extended autonomy agentic session that ultimately produced a good-looking dashboard with nothing but false-alarms. I tried to establish a framework in which other developers could easily add new generative categories and the system would run new fuzzers for them, compare outputs, and triage failures. AI parallelism made for impressive work, but in this early project I was unable to accomplish my goal and gave up on the idea.

Port data sync libraries into PHP

As an experiment in goal-oriented design, ten distributed data structure libraries were ported into PHP userspace code to aid in building a demonstrator for the DE-RTC prototype [#12334, #79602]. With minor caveats, this built working copies of yjs, automerge, loro, diamond-types, diff-match-patch, json-patch, json-joy, sharedb-json0, prosemirror-collab, and collabs which passed their upstream test suites when they were converted to call the PHP code. Eight of the libraries were completed within a few days, but loro (the library I was primarily interested in) and json-joy held out the longest, taking weeks to complete. They appeared stagnant for the bulk of that time and rapidly finished passing the remaining tests in a burst at the end. While I had originally built a prototype collaborative editor with yjs (which is what the existing project team had chosen to use in JavaScript), once automerge completed I was able to swap out the synchronization primitive and later do that again with loro, adding the capability to make more semantically granular changes and merges. This work was almost entirely hands-off and ran in the background until it was completed; every ten minutes it updated an HTML dashboard showing status and operating notes.

Fuzz-test the proposed collaborative editor for WordPress

From the end of April until October, I paired with Dan Luu to fuzz-test the collaborative editor proposal, and we uncovered an array of issues which ultimately led to changes in the timeline for the project, as a number of the defects were nontrivial to solve. Most of the fuzz infrastructure was built by Dan, while I attempted to coordinate the reproducible bug reports with the rest of the team and to propose fixes. The fuzzing machinery produced effectively no false positives due to the triage and reproduction steps built in. It also provided the visuals for theoretical bugs which are hard to diagnose manually with a keyboard and mouse, but which actually occur frequently in concurrent systems.

This was a high-reward project for the investment because, while AI was dominant in the early code generation, once the testing suite was established, it was able to continue to operate without much additional AI input, and it’s possible to run without any AI inputs.

It highlighted two aspects of fuzz-testing: the more robust the code being tested already is, the more valuable the fuzz-testing will be; and the more frequently a bug is likely to materialize, the more quickly fuzz-testing will find it. There is a good match here between the needs and the operating characteristics.

Actually, Dan and I were originally looking at working on other projects for this Radical experiment. I had suggested that we use the nascent collaborative editing project to organize our notes and work within a WordPress site — to “dogfood” the editor. We pivoted to this testing and design support role only because of problems which immediately appeared as we tried to use it.

Prototype a comprehensive collaborative editing environment for WordPress

To demonstrate another approach to collaborative editing, I instructed an agent to follow my core principles and requirements for the task and build a prototype. At first I wanted the agent to mimic forming its own company, planning, dividing labor, and harmonizing productivity, but as this ran for weeks it kept descending into a cycle of producing more and more meaningless paperwork with less and less actual work. Around the end of May I rebooted the project with far more direction and guidance, replacing the goal-oriented and hands-off approach with a human-driving-the-loop method. This proved more effective and in two weeks I had a working prototype that demonstrated every aspect that I considered important and lacking in some of the other public proposals. At some point I will share a version of an internal post I wrote summarizing this work. It proved influential on the project and I believe that the continued development of collaborative editing is heading in a stronger direction as a result.

For years I have struggled to adequately convey why specific principles and requirements are important, but having a visual prototype made it feel real in a way that persuasion had failed me. The amount of up-front work to produce this prototype had been obstructive for years, and without the agent I would not have been able to communicate the tradeoffs involved in its approach.

Restore developer documentation generation by updating deprecated legacy code

At the end of February I had restored WordPress developer documentation which had been stale for two years due to failing build scripts and deploy scripts. While this work resolved most issues and unlocked updated docs for WordPress 6.9, there remained a few unresolved issues which led to specific submodules being excluded from those docs. In mid-May, fixes for the remaining issues were applied to the dependent projects which removed all remaining barriers. All documentation was updatable again and the scripts could run in the latest PHP versions without crashing.

Prevent mistakes in commit messages and automate the repetitive parts of writing them

After seeing my colleague Jon Surrell’s neovim linter for writing WordPress commit messages, I ported his linter into a single-binary/stdout LSP usable in any LSP-supporting editor. This expanded the work Jon did and built upon work from my other tools to show inline previews of Trac tickets and GitHub PRs. It included new auto-fixers for formatting and line ordering and I use this today to prepare my commit messages, avoiding mistakes I have overlooked in the past.

Gather empirical evidence to guide parsing decisions in the HTML API

I used an instrumented custom build of PHP and lexbor in September to answer a perplexing question: “how many tokens of lookahead would be required for the HTML Processor to fully-parse a given percentage of all HTML documents?” This stems from the tricky re-parenting issues in HTML tree building, where a syntax form at the end of the document could appear towards the start of parsed tree structure. The instrumented code examined when lexbor ran its “adoption-agency algorithm” and tracked how much further into the document the current token appeared after the token associated with its actual parent node.

An hour-long run of cc-analyzer showed that among 70,000 documents, approximately 1,000 require at least 1-token lookahead, only about 250 could parse with 5-token lookahead, and 13 would have required more than 10,000-token lookahead! In one case, a document contained an un-closed <b> tag near the start of the document, and then 400 kB and 35,000 syntax tokens later, triggered re-parenting — no default behavior will offer 35,000-token lookahead.

The outcome of this run was disappointing, but the data was invaluable and prevented wasting time implementing a lookahead mechanism that wouldn’t meaningfully benefit consumers of the API.

Review and scrutinize code change proposals

Throughout the entire experiment AI was providing valuable code review and patch preparation. WordPress security fixes are typically backported to WordPress 4.7, which covers 25 released versions and trunk. Many of these support older versions of PHP missing standard-library features that newer code depends on, and lack WordPress functionality that newer code depends on. When preparing a backported patch, I created reports detailing which features and functions had to change at each WordPress release, and what was driving that need. I found these to be more useful than having agents automate the backporting as fewer mistakes were overlooked when I was performing the changes with the assistance of the reports.

AI code review was invaluable though during the refactor of wp_kses() within WordPress. For weeks I instructed it to find the remaining overlooked defects that need resolving before merge, and it kept finding places to harden or fix the code. I never asked an agent to perform “code review” or indicate if a patch was ready to go. Instead, I instructed them to find hidden defects that I wasn’t sure existed, but when told to return three items, they would do it! I consider these kinds of situations among LLMs’ greatest strengths, when false negatives are more costly than false positives, and when validating claims is trivial. Every issue the agent claimed became a test that proved or disproved it and now guards against regression.

Simplenote and Simperium

Implement well-defined feature requests in unfamiliar code

To explore autonomous feature development, I had an agent resolve a concrete bug report describing difficulty copying content from historic revisions of a note [#3358]. This kind of enhancement/fix was frustrating previously because it touches numerous parts of the codebase I was unfamiliar with. The models picked up a number of places I would have overlooked when working on the problem.

Document confusing data flows in unfamiliar projects

The data service powering Simplenote was written with untyped Python code, and partial duck-typed data structures are passed around which can make code comprehension dizzying. While I wanted to avoid AI-generated code changes, given how critical the backend is, in late May I produced comment-only changes annotating data types and providing explanatory comments where certain code constructs were unclear. This was a low-effort way to pass along some insight about the code in hopes that it makes someone else’s job clearer in the future, as I have not maintained this codebase for years.

Random

Monitor Codex usage

codex-usage-report.py scans the ~/.codex directory and summarizes token counts, the models which were used with them, and approximates the dollar cost of that usage based on current API pricing.

Export Codex usage into a searchable format

As the radical experiment was drawing to a close, I created a Codex exporter which dumps the session data into a giant single-file HTML archive where I can search interactively through the sessions and view the chat history, including tool calls, in a rendered view. I’ve referenced this several times as it’s quick and easy compared to logging into a server, finding the right session, and searching through its history.

Run inference on unsupported legacy hardware

My old MacBook Pro came with a dedicated Radeon GPU and sits idle or off most of the time. llama.cpp doesn’t support the older GPU and so I wanted to see if I could get it running. It did produce a working copy that runs local inference on the Radeon GPU, but in practice it underperformed the CPU-based inference for the same models. With only 4 GB of VRAM, it couldn’t load enough weights at one time to operate without constantly transferring data, and the transfer overhead was too high. I explored different means of sharing work between the CPU and GPU, but they were fighting for memory bandwidth.

While this didn’t provide me with a low-and-slow inference engine, it demonstrated the ideas and ran the experiments which is something I had little patience for, given that I expected poor usefulness in the best of cases.

Fix bugs in proprietary hardware drivers

At home I use my Fujifilm X-T3 as a webcam. It makes for a great quality video feed, but when Fujifilm updated the camera driver to integrate with one of the previous macOS updates, they introduced a memory leak which would end up using 90 GB+ of RAM plus swap by the end of a call and sometimes take down my system before I realized it. Knowing I had little hope of motivating Fujifilm to fix this, I made a binary patch to the driver and fixed the bug directly. This was directly inspired by stories of Microsoft fixing bugs in components whose source code they had lost.

To my delight this fixed the memory leak and provided a plausible explanation. By decompiling the driver, the AI found a missing call to release JPEG data from each frame after passing it to CMIOSampleBufferCreate — a classic memory bug. It predicted the impact of this defect and confirmed the rate of memory bloat with successive system dumps of the process. To add the missing release call it shuffled around some existing instructions to a region of padding bytes in the driver and then called into those; this freed up the bytes necessary for the instructions to call the release function. 44 bytes are written across three spans to make the fix, and this is a verifiable fix that I was able to apply without disabling the system integrity protection — an even better delight.

This has been quite possibly my favorite AI-assisted project. There is no way I could have imagined doing this work myself or having traction with Fujifilm to debug and fix this issue, and yet now I can have video calls run on for hours (were I to want such a thing) and memory use by the driver is fixed; it doesn’t fill up and then purge all of my RAM.

A special thanks belongs to Automattic for providing this space in which to learn and explore, to OpenAI who provided elevated access to their frontier models and made it possible to preview what a future of abundant AI might look like, and to the Jetstream2 project funded by US taxpayers who donated high-capacity compute resources to help improve the reliability and security of the WordPress project. I would also like to thank Dan Luu, who worked with me on this project and who taught me so much about practical generative/fuzz testing, and with whom I could never keep pace, in the best of ways.

Over the course of this time period I worked with GPT-5.4 all the way up to GPT-6-Astra, at ultra thinking levels on fast priority, and with Claude Sonnet 4.6–5.4. The earliest use came from Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, but I had also been running Qwen3.5-27B-4bit locally before the experiment started, and by the end was relying on Qwen3.6-27B-4bit.

I’m thankful for the chance to reach into the past and demonstrate ideas I’ve had sitting on the back-burner, as well as to look towards the future and prototype designs I want to see turn into usable products.

We get a lot of flak at WordPress.org for supporting older PHP versions, but an area we’ve always pushed the frontier is in Web Standards, getting websites and browsers evolving together to make the web richer. Ever since I caught the religion from Zeldman, promoting more functionality in the browser has been a life mission.

It’s a little nerdy, but we wanted to do client-side media processing (use all that amazing Apple and Google silicon instead of burdening the poor servers) so we used something amazing Google created called Document Isolation Policy. When WordPress 7.1 “Mary Lou” shipped these features only worked in Chromium-based browsers and Mozilla and Webkit/Apple weren’t keen to support it, but since then Mozilla has expressed support and WebKit has withdrawn their initial concerns. WordPresser Adam Silverstein has been driving much of this work and opened a WICG issue to help move the standard forward and formally requested that WebKit add support.

Hat tip: Anne McCarthy for helping with this post.

(If you want to see other crazy stuff we’re doing in browsers, check out WordPress Playground, I think it’s actually the perfect web development environment for agents, which can then publish to Spacefast.)

On 19th and 20th September 2026, the WordPress community gathered at Civil Service College Uganda, a venue close to River Nile, for the fifth edition of WordCamp Jinja. The event brought together more than 300 diverse participants across 2 days and 3 parallel tracks of sessions full of learning, collaboration and connection. In a city known for its flowing waters, creativity and ideas flowed too, as participants shared their experiences, explored new possibilities with WordPress and built relationships that would carry beyond the weekend.

Our theme, “Embrace Creative Currents on the Nile: Where Inclusivity Fuels Creativity,” reflected the mix of people and ideas in the room. Students sat alongside developers, designers, writers, educators, entrepreneurs and experienced WordPress contributors. Across three parallel tracks, everyone could find a way to learn, share or build.

Students and Creatives at the heart of WordCamp Jinja

Nearly half of this year’s participants were students. Their presence was felt throughout the event, from the speaker sessions to the labs and hackathon tables. We had students from primary schools, secondary schools and universities joining us for this year’s WordCamp.

Some came to explore WordPress for the first time. Others arrived with projects, questions and skills they wanted to develop. Sharing the same spaces with people already working in technology and creative fields gave them an opportunity to learn directly from practitioners and see where their own interests might lead.

One student in attendance found a creative way to remember his experience. Fascinated by the WordPress ecosystem, its generosity and inclusivity, he drew all the sponsor logos by hand so he could remember them after the event. His drawings became a personal record of the community he had encountered at WordCamp Jinja, a small but memorable expression of the curiosity WordCamp Jinja inspired.

Bringing young people into the community has been a continuing part of WordCamp Jinja’s work. Last year’s edition at Jinja Senior Secondary School brought the event closer to students; this year, their participation remained central even at a different venue. We hope the relationships formed over these two days continue at Jinja WordPress Meetups and in the projects students choose to pursue next.

Event highlights

Diverse Speaker Sessions

Our speakers brought different backgrounds and experiences to the stage. Sessions opened up conversations about WordPress and the wider web, including how people use technology to create, teach, solve problems and build livelihoods.

The value of these talks was in the experiences behind them. Speakers shared what they had learned through their own work, answered questions and gave attendees ideas to take back to their studies, organisations and businesses. Thank you to everyone who prepared a session and made the journey to Jinja to share it with us.

Charity Website Hackathon and Contributor Sessions

The Charity Website Hackathon returned as one of WordCamp Jinja’s most practical activities. Participants and facilitators worked together on WordPress projects for organisations seeking to establish or improve their online presence. The teams had to think about real needs: what information a visitor should find, how to organise it and how the organisation could keep its site useful after the event.

For newer participants, this was a chance to learn by working through a real project with support close at hand. For experienced developers and designers, it was a chance to mentor others and put their skills to work for the wider community. The work begun at the hackathon can continue beyond the conference as teams and organisations develop their websites further.

Contributor activities connected that local work to the wider WordPress project. Attendees explored the idea that contributing to open source goes beyond writing code: people can help through photography, translation, testing, documentation, training and community work. There were a lot of new contributors who were taken through the contribution journey by table leads. We hope that for those that took their first steps, WordCamp Jinja will be the beginning of a longer contribution journey.

Hands-on Labs

The Hands-on Labs offered a different pace from the speaker sessions. Instead of only listening, participants could practically follow a facilitator on state of the art computers, try something themselves and ask for help when they needed it.

That kind of guided practice matters, especially for people who are new to a tool or trying to turn an idea into something they can build. Thank you to the facilitators who prepared the activities and worked directly with participants, and to the volunteers who helped make the sessions run.

Memorable moments, connections and networking

Some of the weekend’s most useful moments happened away from the front of a room. Over lunch, in the corridors and between activities, attendees met people from other communities, exchanged ideas and caught up with friends they had met at earlier WordPress events.

For a student attending for the first time, a conversation with a developer or designer can make a possible career feel closer. For returning community members, it was a chance to meet new collaborators and hear perspectives they might otherwise miss. Those connections are part of what keeps WordCamp Jinja going after the closing session.

Celebrating at the Source of the Nile

The celebration continued at Source of the Nile for our after-party, where attendees, volunteers, speakers, facilitators, sponsors and organisers were welcomed to the Source of the Nile. Unbeknownst to them, there was a surprise awaiting: an after party aboard a double-decker boat. The boat ride took them on a tour of Lake Victoria and finally landed at the actual source of the Nile itself, where they learned about its history before taking time for photos together.

The Nile has been part of WordCamp Jinja’s identity across previous editions. This year, gathering there brought our theme back into focus: people with different skills and experiences had come together, learned from one another and added something to the community.

The people who made it possible

WordCamp Jinja is built by volunteers. Long before the doors opened, the organising team was working on the venue, programme, speakers, communications, sponsorships, registration and practical activities. During the event, volunteers welcomed attendees, supported speakers, guided participants and helped the different spaces run smoothly.

To our attendees, thank you for showing up ready to learn and share. To our speakers and facilitators, thank you for the time and care you put into your sessions. To the hackathon teams and contributors, thank you for building and giving back. And to every organiser and volunteer, thank you for the work people saw and the work they did not.

We are also grateful to our sponsors Jetpack, Hostinger, WordPress.com, Woo, Hosting.com, SEOPress and Infinity Computers and Communications Company (i3c) and to our continued local community partners for supporting an accessible gathering for people at different stages of their WordPress journey. Their support helped bring this fifth edition to life.

Relive the weekend and keep in touch


You can explore photographs from the event in our WordCamp Jinja 2026 photo album:
https://photos.app.goo.gl/Fd61HxxyNT8xK4Ni7

WordCamp may be over, but the learning continues. The Jinja WordPress Meetup will keep bringing people together to share skills, contribute to WordPress and build on the projects and relationships started here.

Thank you for embracing the creative currents with us. See you at the next WordPress Jinja event!

bbPress 2.6.20 is a security and maintenance release. Everyone running bbPress should update.

This release strengthens topic and reply password validation and keeps bbPress post shortcodes literal in ordinary WordPress content loops. It also adds a site-wide Forum Status setting with Open, Closed, and Frozen modes. Existing sites remain Open unless that setting is changed.

The maintenance work improves BuddyPress profile actions, group topic routes, activity visibility, and group-forum access. It also restores compatibility for subscription links in third-party theme packages, preserves moderation forms after validation errors, and includes fixes for notifications, converters, widgets, profiles, topic and reply administration, and restricted-content visibility.

bbPress 2.6.20 still requires WordPress 6.0 or newer and PHP 7.2 or newer, and is tested through WordPress 7.1. The database version remains 264, so no database upgrade is required. The 2.6.20 upgrade notes cover compatibility details.

These changes are also in the 2.7 development branch, which remains 2.7.0-alpha-4. Thank you to ahillmortons, alejandroescobar89, bor0, bradleyt, chefranov, dd32, deborah86, Dermes, diegootgs, dilip2615, fraph24, hardel, imath, immeet94, iworks, jgasba, josephscott, konnektiv, lmstearn, mehrazmorshed, michael8888, mike80222, obenland, Palagrin, peopleinside, r-a-y, robin-w, SirLouen, tobifjellner, wpturk, and zaerl for reports, patches, testing, and review.

Download bbPress 2.6.20 from WordPress.org, or update from your WordPress dashboard.

[00:00:19] Nathan Wrigley: Welcome to the Jukebox Podcast from WP Tavern. My name is Nathan Wrigley.

Jukebox is a podcast which is dedicated to all things WordPress. The people, the events, the plugins, the blocks, the themes, and in this case, the state of WordPress security in 2026, and the battle against AI threats.

If you’d like to subscribe to the podcast, you can do that by searching for WP Tavern in your podcast player of choice, or by going to wptavern.com/feed/podcast, and you can copy that URL into most podcast players.

If you have a topic that you’d like us to feature on the podcast, I’m keen to hear from you, and hopefully get you, or your idea, featured on the show. Head to wptavern.com/contact/jukebox and use the form there.

So on the podcast today we have Robert Abela.

Robert has been working in IT security for 25 years, ranging from antivirus software to web security scanners, and for the past decade has been running Melapress. A company focused on WordPress security plugins, particularly around user visibility, authentication, activity logs, and 2FA.

Robert is here to talk about the 2026 WordPress security survey. This is an annual project now in its fourth, or fifth, year gathering data from a wide range of WordPress professionals across agencies, enterprise teams, freelancers, and product owners. The conversation today is focused on the biggest security challenges and trends facing WordPress users in 2026.

We start off with some sobering stats. Over 67% of survey respondents reported experiencing at least one security incident in the past year, and concerns about WordPress security remain high, especially among less technical users.

We chat about the disconnect between awareness of security threats and actually taking steps to mitigate them, such as breach recovery plans and team training.

The discussion also explored the different types of risks that worry site owners. Site downtime, defacement, reputational damage, data loss, and even legal compliance issues. How the shakeout depends on the type of site, whether it’s e-commerce membership, a news outlet, or a simple brochure site.

We also talk about the tendency for even experienced WordPress users to take a reactive approach, only addressing vulnerabilities after something has gone wrong.

Towards the end of the episode, we discuss the rising impact of a AI on security, the explosion of AI facilitated vulnerabilities, and the shifting landscape of risk and response. There’s a healthy dose of reality, some optimism about the tools and best practises available, and plenty of good advice, especially for smaller teams and freelancers who may not have access to enterprise level resources.

If you care about keeping your WordPress sites secure, or want to understand where the community’s biggest concerns and opportunities are in 2026, this episode is for you.

If you’re interested in finding out more, you can find all of the links in the show notes by heading to wptavern.com/podcast where you’ll find all the other episodes as well.

[00:26:44] Nathan Wrigley: It’s such a curious industry that you’re in because, how to describe this? It would seem, or at least, it would be possible to perceive that this security survey is perfectly aligned with your business goals in a way. There’s loads of problems out there on the internet. There’s multitudes of ways that things can go wrong, and for every one of them, there’s, a WordPress solution out there.

But I know Robert. We’ve met many times before. I get the intuition that’s really not why you’re doing this, although somebody listening to this might have that sort of slightly, I don’t know, cynical approach that, Robert’s just saying this so that he can launch his Melapress products at you. Just put our minds to rest on that score. Why do you actually carry out this survey?

[00:27:25] Robert Abela: Good question. Actually, our plugins only address part of the security. There’s much more when it comes to firewalls, et cetera, that I still say hardening you still need. We don’t even cover it.

No, we do it, honestly, it started around four or five years ago, for me, it was just curiosity. It sounded like an interesting to do. Hey, let’s do a survey, just experimenting, et cetera. And we had very good response, and now we’re just, doing it honestly.

Like I really believe that by knowing, this is not just about WordPress security, about everything else. By knowing where other people are doing it wrong, you will learn from it. By knowing, okay, clearly I can see, for example, as we were saying, like seventy percent, seventy point two percent of enterprise and marked businesses usually have logs, usually have firewalls, et cetera. Maybe we should aspire more towards them and be more like the average website should have a bit more like things like that, and maybe they’re doing something right.

So yes, there is a lot to learn from surveys in general, not just this, any type of survey. There is usually a lot to learn. And that’s why we’re doing it as well, because from the first time we’ve done it, which started really as a curiosity project, we got so much good feedback. And actually the second year people were asking us if we are going to do it. Because yeah, people learn from these things.

I mean, of course there’s the benefit of it, hopefully it will promote as well a bit our plugins. But anyway, it’s going to promote all other type of security solutions. We are not, in fact, the survey is not tailored just for our plugin. It talks about everything. As I said, the whole security cycle. You have the hardening, you have the monitoring, updating, et cetera, and we only do one part of it, the monitoring aspect, basically.

[00:28:50] Nathan Wrigley: Before we move on to our sort of final bit, which I want to concentrate on AI, I’m just going to wrap up the security bit just by summarizing what comes towards the end. And it’s less about numbers, and it’s more about just conclusions that may have been drawn. But most of it, I think, would be fairly obvious from what we said. So I’ll just summarize it a little bit.

The first one is that e-commerce and membership sites tend to have greater security concerns and stronger practices. That kind of makes sense. I guess it reflects the nature of the business they’re in, and the kind of data that they’re holding, and the legal compliance that they may need to be concerend with.

In-house teams are more likely to have recovery plans. Again, I presume that’s fairly obvious. The boss, the head of the pyramid can sit down and say, “Okay, it’s your job now to crack on and do that. You’ve got a week to figure out all this sort of stuff,” and what have you. Whereas a freelancer sitting in their own office, there’s always regular work to be built, sites to be built and other things to do. So I can well imagine why that’s the case.

And sites, again, fairly obvious, sites with repeated security incidents tended to have stronger controls in place. Today, presumably, it’s a case of once bitten and all of that. Once you’ve actually had this nasty stuff happen to you, you’re pretty likely to make sure that does not happen again.

In summary, I suppose the reports really, the recommendations are focus on prevention, detection, and recovery rather than simply adding in more security tools, would be the way that I would describe it.

Okay, let’s move on then just before we finish. It is, as we’re recording this, it’s September 2026. In the more recent past, I want to say, I don’t know, the last two months, something like that, the WordPress security news bulletins have been on red alert really. We’ve had some charts being put out on social media which show the amount of vulnerabilities discovered, and also the amount of AI-based plugins that have gone into the repository. The supply chain attacks that have suddenly become a thing. A lot of it really because people can corral AI to do mischievous stuff and what have you.

I don’t really have a question, but I just wondered if you had a comment on where we are in September 2026, because it does feel as if there’s quite a lot of, there’s a lot of scope to be very doomer at the moment. It almost feels like the AI is winning the arms race, but maybe that’s not what you’re thinking from your end.

[00:31:04] Robert Abela: No, it looks a bit negative. I wouldn’t say AI is winning the race. Actually, people with malicious intent using AI are winning because AI is neutral in a way, like it depends on what people ask the AI to do.

[00:31:15] Nathan Wrigley: Yes.

[00:31:16] Robert Abela: But it is worrying, yes. The graph you are mentioning, I saw a graph shared by John Blackbourn, yeah, about the number of issues reported in the HackerOne WordPress vulnerability program, which is insane.

[00:31:28] Nathan Wrigley: Yes.

[00:31:29] Robert Abela: And they received more reports in the last week than they ever did in a whole number of months. So yes, it is worrying. You can look at it both ways. The same way attackers can use AI to find issues. We are doing it ourselves as well, quite frankly, because whenever there’s a new model out there from all of these vendors, most probably attackers are going to use them to scan our code, et cetera. So we’re doing it as well.

We always used to do the manual security analysis, et cetera, but now that we have AI, with every release, we just hammer the update and try to find as many issues as we can.

The reality is also that some, if not many of these vulnerabilities are not actually so easy to exploit. Like it’s really, the stars really have to align and it’s really, but still, it’s better safe than sorry. Because even though today it might be difficult to exploit a particular issue, in six months’ time, we might have technology that might make it very easy to exploit this type of issue.

[00:35:13] Nathan Wrigley: Yeah, the bit that genuinely I find curious is what will be the calculus in terms of time that people can spend on this stuff. [00:36:10] Robert Abela: Yes. Yes, it’s the reality. [00:37:07] Nathan Wrigley: Yeah, it will be interesting in the face of AI vulnerability. It’d be interesting to see what the, let’s say hosting companies, let’s paint a target there. [00:37:58] Robert Abela: Yes, I’m active on LinkedIn, Robert Abela. I’m active on X.com, and I finally also have my own website. It’s more on personal things quite frankly, but yeah, it’s robertabela.me.

[00:38:08] Nathan Wrigley: In which case I will bury those in the bottom of the show notes as well.

[00:38:12] Robert Abela: Thanks.

[00:38:12] Nathan Wrigley: So that you can find those. Robert Abela, thank you for chatting to me today. I really appreciate it.

[00:38:16] Robert Abela: Thanks likewise.

On the podcast today we have Robert Abela.

Robert has been working in IT security for 25 years, ranging from antivirus software to web security scanners, and for the past decade has been running Melapress, a company focused on WordPress security plugins, particularly around user visibility, authentication, activity logs, and 2FA.

Robert is here to talk about the 2026 WordPress Security Survey, this is an annual project, now in its fourth or fifth year, gathering data from a wide range of WordPress professionals across agencies, enterprise teams, freelancers, and product owners. The conversation today is focused on the biggest security challenges and trends facing WordPress users in 2026.

We start off with some sobering stats, over 67% of survey respondents reported experiencing at least one security incident in the past year, and concerns about WordPress security remain high, especially among less technical users. We chat about the disconnect between awareness of security threats and actually taking steps to mitigate them, such as breach recovery plans and team training.

The discussion also explored the different types of risks that worry site owners, site downtime, defacement, reputational damage, data loss, and even legal compliance issues, how these shake out depends on the type of site, whether it’s e-commerce, membership, a news outlet, or a simple brochure site.

We also talk about the tendency for even experienced WordPress users to take a reactive approach, only addressing vulnerabilities after something has gone wrong.

Towards the end of the episode, we discuss the rising impact of AI on security, the explosion of AI-facilitated vulnerabilities, and the shifting landscape of risk and response. There’s a healthy dose of reality, some optimism about the tools and best practices available, and plenty of good advice, especially for smaller teams and freelancers who may not have access to enterprise-level resources.

If you care about keeping your WordPress sites secure, or want to understand where the community’s biggest concerns and opportunities are in 2026, this episode is for you.

Almost a third of our source code was comments. I deleted all of them and asked an AI agent to build the same features on both versions of the codebase, three times each. The code it wrote was just as good with or without comments.

If you use agents on a real codebase and wonder whether comments help them, slow them down, or don’t matter, here’s what I found.

Why I tried this

In this video (around 23:07), Lauren mentions that they don’t let their agents write comments in the code. Our codebase, is the opposite: it’s full of comments, and most of them were written by agents.

So I wondered: are all those comments helping the agent, or are they just extra text it has to read?

The experiment in one paragraph

I made a copy of the codebase with every comment removed, about 168,000 lines in total. Then I gave the same task to the same agent on both copies, three times on each, and checked the results the same way. I did this for two tasks, a small one and a bigger one.

The results

Every run passed every check: lint, type checks and the existing tests, plus, on the bigger task, a hidden test the agent never saw. A separate AI judge scored each result without knowing which copy it came from (more on that below).

Small task: tile all open windows (score out of 19)

Bigger task: keep a window on top (score out of 23)

The numbers are averages of three runs. The score differences are within noise, and so is the cost on the bigger task. On the small task, the agent used about 22% fewer tokens without comments, which makes sense: there was simply less to read.

The bigger task had a trap. The pinned state has to survive a page reload, and the PHP function that saves the window session drops any key it doesn’t know. Miss it and the feature looks fine until you reload. That’s exactly the kind of thing you’d expect a comment to help with. All six runs found it, with and without comments.

Why one run is not enough

My first plan was to run each branch once. I’m glad I didn’t.

On the bigger task, the three runs with comments used 8.21M, 8.79M and 10.17M tokens. The three runs without comments used 7.01M, 9.70M and 10.64M.

If I had picked one run from each branch, I could have written two opposite blog posts. Comparing 10.64M with 8.21M, removing comments makes the agent 30% more expensive. Comparing 7.01M with 10.17M, it makes the agent 31% cheaper. Same task, same code, same day.

Agents are not deterministic. If you’re measuring one, run it more than once.

How I ran it

  • The agent: Claude Code with Opus 5.5 at high effort. Same model and settings for every run.
  • The two codebases: our main branch, and a copy with the comments removed. I compiled both and checked that the resulting code is identical. The only comments left are the ones the tools need to work, such as lint directives and plugin headers, about 800 lines.
  • The tasks: two real features, with the same prompt on both branches.
  • The checks: the project’s own lint, type checks and tests. On the bigger task, also a hidden test I added after the agent finished, so it couldn’t write code just to pass it.
  • The judge: a separate Claude session read each change and scored it against a checklist written before the runs: does it work, does it follow the project’s conventions, does it have tests, and so on. The changes were labelled with random names, so the judge didn’t know which branch each one came from.
  • The runs: three per branch per task, alternating branches so that time of day affected both equally.

My conclusion

For the agent, code comments don’t make a difference to the quality of the code it writes. They don’t help, and they don’t hurt.

So keep a comment or delete it based on what it does for the people reading the code, not for the agent.

This doesn’t prove comments have zero effect. I tested one model, two tasks and three runs per branch, which is enough to rule out a big effect, not a small one.

Next: comments made no difference, but removing our docs/ folder and AGENTS.md did. That’s the next post.

Speaking of sci-fi authors, Automattic is hosting Neal Stephenson for a livestream about his new book soon, please tune in!

Neal was a big influence on WordPress! I got hip to him from Tantek. In the source code of billions of pages you’ll see this:

<link rel="profile" href="https://gmpg.org/xfn/11">

GMPG is the Global Media Protocols Group, “an experiment in Metamemetics.” Inspired, of course, by the Global Multimedia Protocol Group that owned the virtual real estate in Snow Crash’s metaverse.

Eric, Tantek, and I were reacting to the idea that there should be a separate heavily-marked-up RDF or XML web, and that HTML couldn’t be extended or enriched with metadata in a way that was beautiful to both humans and machines. It was really an aesthetic war. (It later got more built out in Microformats.)

We should revisit some of those principles because the web could use more distribution right now.

I’ve been wondering how far a theme can take OpenStation. Not just a wallpaper and a different color, but everything: windows, dock, menus, fonts, icons, layouts, etc. So I tried to make wp-admin look like two operating systems from a long time ago.

Retro 95 reimagines wp-admin as Windows 95. It even comes with a Start menu! And the classic clock sitting in the bottom-right corner is also there. You can try it live.

Retro 84 is the counterpart for Apple fans. It turns wp-admin into the first graphical OS that many people ever saw: the original Macintosh’s System 1. The beloved monochrome display, the classic pixelated font, and more! Check out the live demo.

And here’s a fun fact: every icon is pixel art typed into a text file, one character per pixel. The fonts were also made the same way, letter by letter.

Underneath, it’s the same wp-admin as always, just a few decades older.

If you want to build your own theme, the docs list everything a theme can change. Maybe it’s time for a proper Windows Vista comeback.

[00:00:19] Nathan Wrigley: Welcome to the Jukebox Podcast from WP Tavern. My name is Nathan Wrigley.

Jukebox is a podcast which is dedicated to all things WordPress. The people, the events, the plugins, the blocks, the themes, and in this case, making WordPress the source of truth across web projects, not just the website.

If you’d like to subscribe to the podcast, you can do that by searching for WP Tavern in your podcast player of choice, or by going to wptavern.com/feed/podcast, and you can copy that URL into most podcast players.
